A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

metas.title: License plate
metas.description: Old license plates in Argentina have a black dot in the middle of a white plate, which is easy to spot. New license plates are fully white with a blue line at the top, similar to those in Brazil.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: Landscape - Cordoba Mountains
metas.description: These mountains are typically found west of Córdoba.

metas.title: Landscape - Ushuaia
metas.description: These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia.

metas.title: Landscape - Mountains
metas.description: Far western Argentina typically features a mountainous landscape.

metas.title: Vegetation - Red Baron - Dense
metas.description: Red Baron is a grass species that has a very distinctive red hue.
metas.comparison: In very dense assemblages, it can appear here:

metas.title: Infrastructure - Comodoro Rivadavia Taxi
metas.description: This all white taxi with a black logo is unique to Comodoro Rivadavia.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Tucuman Pole ID
metas.description: White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Resistencia Taxi
metas.description: Taxis with a red-white-green stripe (hungarian flag) are unique to Resistencia.

metas.title: Landscape - Grassland
metas.description: Grassland with a few separated tree plantations is generally found in this area.

metas.title: Vegetation - Single Row Poplar - Flat
metas.description: Poplar Trees are thin and tall decidiuous trees. They can be found all over Argentina.
metas.comparison: If you see them planted in a single row and accompanied by a very flat landscape, you are in one of these places:

metas.title: Landscape - Flat & Barren Landscape
metas.description: Flat and barren landscapes like this are typically found in central southern Argentina.

metas.title: Landscape - Chenque Hill
metas.description: Comodoro Rivadavia is built on the slopes of Chenque hill, making the city recognisable.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Bariloche Taxi
metas.description: This taxi with the white body, blue roof and blue logo is unique to the city of Bariloche.

metas.title: Car Meta - Sawdust Car Meta
metas.description: The “sawdust” car is found in centre-south Argentina and has a unique sandy dust on its visible black back.

metas.title: Landscape - Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino Dam
metas.description: This unique dam with the rock formations typical for Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino can be found west of the town.

metas.title: Landscape - Road of Death
metas.description: The western part of the RN65 in western Tucumán can easily be recognized by this bendy unpaved road up in the mountains.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Sunrise Coverage with Blurs
metas.description: Sunrise coverage with bad image quality and multiple blurs is found on a short part of the RN251 and RN22, west of Río Colorado.

metas.title: Infrastructure - km-marker
metas.description: Argentinian kilometer markers are typically white with a black strip displaying the road number at the top. RN stands for ruta national (white on the map), RP stands for ruta provincial (green on the map).

metas.title: Architecture - Mar del Plata Architecture
metas.description: In Mar Del Plata and surrounding cities (such as Miramar and Necochea), a unique style of architecture can be found. Its main features include quartzite stoned facades, orange tiled roofs, attached garages, and vault shaped porches.

general_rules.text: T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these yellow rectangular signs, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, and the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.

Salta.text: Red taxis with a black stripe are unique to Salta.
These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.
The Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus) can be found in cities in northern Salta such as Orán, Tartagal and General Mosconi.

Jujuy.text: Salt pans in Argentina are typically found in Jujuy.
Wild sunflowers (Verbesina encelioides) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.
Red bricks, similar to what is common in Bolivia, can be found in the northwest of the country, especially in western Jujuy.
Wild sunflowers (Tithonia tubaeformis) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.

Misiones.text: Red soil is typically found in the Misiones province.

The Macaw Palm has small thin leaves with a visible spear shaped top. It can be found as a decorational plant all across Argentina, however in the wild it is most common in Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.
Red soil is typically found in the Misiones province. NOTE: Brazil and Argentina can look similar in this region. Make sure to look for other clues first.

The Macaw Palm has small thin leaves with a visible spear shaped top. It can be found as a decorational plant all across Argentina, however in the wild it is most common in Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.

San Juan.text: White taxis with a yellow roof are unique to San Juan.
This horse trekker can be found in southwestern San Juan.

Cordoba.text: You can find these unique markers on provincial roads in Cordoba.
These all green or all yellow taxis with an oval shape beneath the driver door are unique to Cordoba.
Taxis in Neuquen are all yellow. What distinguishes them from Cordoba taxis is that their doors have no logos or paintings on them.
You can find these unique markers on provincial roads in Cordoba.

Tierra del Fuego.text: Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.
If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.
If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.
Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.

Santiago del Estero.text: White taxis with light-green roofs are unique to Santiago del Estero.
Corn fields can be found in most of northern Argentina, however they are most common in Córdoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero.
Corn fields can be found in most of northern Argentina, however they are most common in Córdoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero.

Santa Cruz.text: This snow coverage is found on the eastern RP25 in eastern Santa Cruz.
Melting snow coverage is seen on the eastern RN293 close to the Chilean border in southwestern Santa Cruz.

Buenos Aires.text: Small lakes near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.
Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.
Fields of sunflowers are mainly found in southern Chaco, and less commonly in Buenos Aires and southern Córdoba.
Fields of sorghum can most commonly be seen in Santa Fe, Córdoba and Buenos Aires. It can be identified by its dark red flowerheads.
Taxis in Jujuy have a black body and a yellow roof. Notably, only the top of the roof is yellow, making it distinct from Rosario or Buenos Aires taxis.
This black and yellow taxi is unique to Mendoza. Jujuy, Rosario and Buenos Aires also have black and yellow taxis, but on those taxis, the body is completely black.

Taxis in Rosario have a black body and a yellow roof. The outer bars are yellow, while the middle bar (behind the driver) is black. This makes them distinguishable from taxis in Jujuy and Buenos Aires.

This taxi with a black body and yellow roof is common in Buenos Aires. Note that taxis from Jujuy and Rosarío have the same combination. However, Buenos Aires is the only city where the taxi has the middle bar (behind the driver) painted.
Small lakes near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.
Fields of sorghum can most commonly be seen in Santa Fe, Córdoba and Buenos Aires. It can be identified by its dark red flowerheads.
Fields of sunflowers are mainly found in southern Chaco, and less commonly in Buenos Aires and southern Córdoba.

Entre Rios.text: The majority of tree plantations in Argentina are located in the Entre Rios province.
The Butia yatay palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline with varying heights. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar, Entre Rios.
The majority of tree plantations in Argentina are located in the Entre Rios province. NOTE: Uruguay and southern Brazil have them as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.
The Butia yatay palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline with varying heights. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar, Entre Rios.

Mendoza.text: In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.
Sunset coverage with degraded image quality is found on the RN40 just south of the Mendoza border with Neuquén.
If you see vineyards with mountains in the west and flatness in the east, you are most likely in the outskirts of Mendoza.
Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.
In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.

San Luis.text: Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.
White taxis with two light-blue stripes (resembling the Argentinian flag) are unique to San Luis.

Trithrinax Campestris, or the caranday palm, not to be confused with the Caranday Wax Palm, is a rustic palm native to the Sierras de Córdoba with a broader distribution in San Luis and northern mountainous Argentina. It can be identified by its compact fan-like leaves with a trunk hidden by a coat of dead-leaves.
Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.

It can be identified by its compact fan-like leaves with a trunk hidden by a coat of dead-leaves.

La Rioja.text: Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.
Red soil with a barren landscape and mountain ranges, can often be seen on the RN76 in Parque Nacional Talampaya in western La Rioja.

Tucuman.text: These old-school, white taxis with a yellow-black checkerboard stripe are unique to Tucuman.

Chubut.text: Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by these rock formations.

Patagonia.text:
Azorella Prolifera is a plant that looks like "cushions". It is found throughout Patagonia.
It's appearence depends on season.

You can see this plant in a distinctive light green color in these regions:

Formosa.text: In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.

Catamarca.text: These volcanic rocks in Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the RP43 south of Antofagasta de la Sierra in northwestern Catamarca.

Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.

Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.

La Pampa.text: Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa.
T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these yellow rectangular signs, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, and the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.

Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa. NOTE: This tree can sometimes be confused with other trees such as the White Carob.

Neuquen.text: The monkey puzzle tree can be found in western Neuquen. The most specimens are seen on provincial road 23 + offroads, between Caviahue and Atreuco.
The RP1 in Neuquen has dark, cloudy coverage. It is a dark red dirt road and thus resembles Mars. There is some spill onto the RP7 in the North and the RP10 in the South.
Single rows of poplar trees, characterised by their thin and tall appearance, are very common around Neuquén. The area is also very flat.

Pampas.text: Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.
Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.

Corrientes.text: Coperinicia alba, also known as the Caranday Wax Palm, have short, fan-like leaves that tend to grow in low-density, single-species forests. Most common in Formosa, they can also be found in Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.

Coperinicia alba, also known as the Caranday Wax Palm, have short, fan-like leaves that tend to grow in low-density, single-species forests. Most common in Formosa, they can also be found in Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.

Chaco.text: In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.

spotlight.text: Red bricks, similar to what is common in Bolivia, can be found in the northwest of the country, especially in western Jujuy.
The Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus) can be found in cities in northern Salta such as Orán, Tartagal and General Mosconi.
Salt pans in Argentina are typically found in Jujuy. NOTE: They can also be found in southwestern Bolivia and northeastern Chile.
These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.
These volcanic rocks in Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the RP43 south of Antofagasta de la Sierra in northwestern Catamarca.
Red soil with a barren landscape and mountain ranges, can often be seen on the RN76 in Parque Nacional Talampaya in western La Rioja.
These mountains are typically found west of Córdoba. NOTE: They are not as high as the mountains in the west.
This horse trekker can be found in southwestern San Juan. NOTE: A similar trekker can be found on the other side in Chile.

If you see vineyards with mountains in the west and flatness in the east, you are most likely in the outskirts of Mendoza. NOTE: There are multiple wine regions in Argentina, but the Mendoza wine region is the most recognisable one of them all.
Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.
The monkey puzzle tree can be found in western Neuquen. The most specimens are seen on state road 23. NOTE: They are seen on the other side in Chile as well.
Sunrise coverage with degraded image quality is found on the RN40 just south of the Mendoza border with Neuquén. NOTE: The quality of the coverage improves closer to the border.
Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by these rock formations. NOTE: Sometimes you will be able to see this dam in the west.
This snow coverage is found on the eastern RP25 in eastern Santa Cruz.
Melting snow coverage is seen on the eastern RN293 close to the Chilean border in southwestern Santa Cruz.
These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia. NOTE: Ushuaia is the southernmost city of Argentina and the province capital of Tierra del Fuego.

AU.name: Australia
AU.key_meta: Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back.
metas.comparison: Turkish bollards are similar but lack a back reflector. If unsure, check the sun position, landscape, or vegetation.

metas.title: Give way sign
metas.description: Give-way signs in Australia have a white border and black text, while in New Zealand, they have red text.

metas.title: Melbourne white blue sticker
metas.description: Those white-blue stickers on poles are unique to Melbourne in Australia.

metas.title: Vic pole top
metas.description: Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top.(sometimes might be missing the top one)

metas.title: Infrastructure - South Australia Bus Stop
metas.description: Orange signpost, sign extending over the signpost.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Gold Coast Streetsign
metas.description: This street sign is unique to Gold Coast City Council.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Darwin Bus Stop
metas.description: The city of Darwin, NT uses concrete shelters as bus stops.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Tasmania Bus Stop
metas.description: Different versions, but usually have "Metro" written on them.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Mount Kosciuszko
metas.description: All-yellow road lines can be seen on roads around Mount Kosciuszko.
metas.comparison: In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Octagonal Pole
metas.description: Octagonal Poles in Australia are found mostly in and around Sydney.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Jervis Bay Meta
metas.description: Jervis Bay only has Gen 1 coverage, all of which has a 2021 copyright.

metas.title: Landscape - Tom Price Landscape
metas.description: The area around Tom Price can be recognized by its red soil and rocky hills.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Western Australia Bus Stop
metas.description: Bus Stops in Australia are marked by these horizontal poles with information on them.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Blue Square on Pole
metas.description: Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.

metas.title: Landscape - Mount Gambier Tree Plantations
metas.description: The area around Mount Gambier, SA features white soil and extensive pine tree plantations, making it recognisable.

metas.title: Landscape - Nullarbor Highway
metas.description: The Nullarbor Highway (Latin for “no tree”) can be easily recognized thanks to the flatness, overall grey look and very low vegetation.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Use the road angle or road lines to determine whether you are on the WA or SA side.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Western Australia License Plate
metas.description: Western Australian License Plate have blue letters and a thin blue stripe at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.

metas.title: Landscape - Stuart Highway with Blue Car
metas.description: The Stuart Highway from Alice Springs to around Pimba, SA can be easily recognized by its bright orange dirt, short trees and blue car Generation 4.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Sloped Kerbs
metas.description: You can sometimes see sloped kerbs in Perth, where it gradually declines to the road, whilst in other cities kerbs go straight down at a 90 degree angle.

metas.title: Landscape - Darwin Landscape
metas.description: The vegetation in the area surrounding Darwin is extremely distinct. It features dark red soil, as well as rich green grass and trees. The tree trunks are typically black.

metas.title: Landscape - Green & Golden Fields
metas.description: Lush green or golden fields can be found in this band from the south of the Yorke Peninsula to Echuca. In the SA side, the landscape should be drier than the Victorian side and more wide crowned eucalyptus can be seen. On the Victorian side, the trees generally have more leaves and are taller.

general_rules.text: Different states use different licence plate designs, which can be somewhat visible through the blur.
Australian phone numbers are 8 digits with a 2-digit area code in front. A map of these by state can be seen here. Keep in mind, not all phone numbers will include an area code in front of it.

Roads that start with the letter ‘C’ are only found in Victoria and Tasmania. In addition, South Australia has some C roads near the border with Victoria. NOTE: Since these are smaller and less major roads, Generation 1 or 2 is common.

Western Australia.text: Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia.
Black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
Bollards with brown paint at the bottom are most commonly found in Western Australia.
You can find these dark green property markers on the sides of roads in Western Australia.

You can only find flat signposts in South Australia and Western Australia (in WA they mostly will be yellow but not always). You will also find rounded sign posts in SA (so don't rule SA if you see rounded one).
These brush plants are commonly seen in Western Australia.
These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round.
Western Australia, and especially the Perth area, is known for its reddish-orange soil.
A sun with "splodges" around it can be observed on the 95 in Western Australia, between Newman and Ex Doolgunna.
A trident-like pole top with the insulators pointing to the top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.
Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.
The town of Gascoyne Junction in Western Australia is distinct, as the driver left the car boot open while covering this town, creating a very unique car meta.

Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia.

In addition, the island only has Generation 2 and Generation 4 coverage, with Generation 2 being most common.
Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.

Bollards with brown paint at the bottom are most commonly found in Western Australia. NOTE: Brown paint at the bottom of exposed bollards can also rarely be seen in other states, however the brown section will not be as large.
These black-and-white stripy bollards are unique to Western Australia.
Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia. NOTE: Although South Australia does not use yellow signposts for regular road signs, SA bus stops will have yellow posts.
Some signposts in South Australia and Western Australia are flat rather than round. NOTE: These signposts are usually yellow in Western Australia.
You can find these dark green property markers on the sides of roads in Western Australia.

Western Australia, and especially the Perth area, is known for its reddish-orange soil. NOTE: Although this is very useful, there are numerous areas in WA with light soil, and conversely there are areas in other states with reddish-orange soil.
These brush plants are commonly seen in Western Australia.

New South Wales.text: New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs.
Guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.
This poletag with 'HP' is found in New South Wales.
This Green Dot on poles is sometimes found in New South Wales.
Blue plates on Taxis are found exclusively in New South Wales.
These poles with hanging insulators are found in Queensland and New South Wales.
These round concrete poles with dots going up on them are found in New South Wales.
In New South Wales, especially in Sydney, some stop signs have three big holes making it unique for this region.
This poletag which consists of rectangular yellow stickers that usually form a T, is exclusive to New South Wales.
Within New South Wales, purely horizontal poletags (i.e. no vertical on the same pole), are not found around Sydney.
This guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.
The ∀-Poletop is found in South Australia and New South Wales. In SA, the pole will be a stobie pole, while in NSW it will be round.
New South Wales uses these two designs for bus stops. One is blue and has a white B in a circle with it, the other has the signpost bending over the actual sign.
Very slim license plate (similar to Swiss front plates) are found in Victoria and New South Wales. While in Victoria, you can usually see two blue blocks of texts, in NSW they appear plain.

Yellow license plates can occasionally be found in New South Wales. Most license plates are still white, though. The old design of Western Australian plates is also yellow, so you might stumble upon them in WA very rarely.

South Australia.text:
If you see gap and reflector in between outer lines you gonna be in ACT.

(South Australia might have gaps in outerlines but reflector in a gap is super rare there)
You can find these white property markers on the sides of roads in South Australia.
The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia.(A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania - super rare)
Poletops that resemble the cyrillic letter ш are unique to South Australia.
South Australia is the only Australian state that uses a 25 speed limit in school zones.
Reflectors that are shorter than the regular ones are most common in Queensland and South Australia.
In South Australia and the ACT, you can sometimes find gaps in the outer roadlines. If this gap has no reflector, it is South Australia.
Roads that start with the letter ‘C’ are only found in Victoria and Tasmania. In addition, South Australia has some C roads near the border with Victoria.
The upper half of a leaf can sometimes be seen on the Generation 2 halo in southeastern South Australia. If it's an entire leaf, it is in Eastern Victoria.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has quite dry vegetation and is made up of shrubs and wide cronwed eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a white tint.

Western South Australia has a similar landscape, but with orangish soil.

The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. The pole tops (trident or rotated letter “E”) are also unique. NOTE: A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania.

Reflectors that are shorter in height than the regular ones are most common in Queensland and South Australia. NOTE: Short reflectors can be found in every state, but are much less common outside of QLD and SA.
South Australia is the only Australian state that uses a 25 speed limit in school zones.
You can find these white property markers on the sides of roads in South Australia.

NSW.text: If you see more than couple yellow plates in Australia you should be in NSW

Within NSW, regular vertical poletags are found south and west of Sydney.

Note that if the poletags have white ends on each side, they are NOT close to Sydney, but rather throughout the rest of NSW.
In Generation 2 coverage in an area of Eastern NSW, a twig is visible in the Generation 2 halo.
In NSW, poletags in the triangle formed by Sydney, Newcastle and Scone (view map) almost always have one or two letters in their codes.
Within NSW, these vertical plates with white ends are not found near Sydney. Note that otherwise, vertical plates will be close to Sydney within NSW.
The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines. They can also be found on other major roads in NSW, such as the Gwydir Highway.

Traffic lights with a white outline around the frame are found in the eastern and western states of WA, QLD, NSW, ACT and Tas. Traffic lights without a border are found in the remaining, central states.
New South Wales is the only state to use red ‘No Stopping’ signs. NOTE: All other states use white versions.

Traffic lights with a white outline around the frame are found in the eastern and western states of WA, QLD, NSW, ACT and Tas. Traffic lights without a border are found in the remaining, central states.
This guardrail ending, featuring a black dash on a yellow background, is almost exclusive to New South Wales and the ACT.

The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.

Northern Territory.text: Rusty metal holey poles are unique to Northern Territory state in Australia.
Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.
Traffic lights without a border are found in Northern Territory, South Australia and Victoria.
Around the Devils Marbles, north of Davenport in the Northern Territory, smoke from a bushfire is visible.
Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.
These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory, and rarely the northern part of Western Australia.
Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does not include an arrow.
The sand palm is endemic to the north of the Northern Territory of Australia, from the Fitzmaurice River to Cape Arnhem and inland as far as Katherine.
On most of the Northern Territory section of the Barkly Highway and a small part of the Queensland section, a wire can be seen on the left side of the car.
Generation 2 coverage cannot be found in Northern Territory. It can also help in 50/50s between Victoria and Tasmania, where Gen 2 is more common in Tasmania.
Termite mounds can sometimes be seen in the Northern Territory and rarely northern WA and QLD. They appear as brown, spiky formations rising out of the ground.
License Plates in Northern Territory have bright red lettering which shines through the blur. Looks kind of similar to the Queensland plates, which are a bit darker.
Alice Springs, an isolated town in the southern part of the Northern Territory, features distinct orange rocks that can be seen in the distance or at the end of roads.
These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory. NOTE: These poles can also sometimes be found in some areas of northern WA, such as Wyndham.
Signposts in the Northern Territory can feature these yellow stickers.
Within Australia, a speed limit of 130 km/h can only be found in the Northern Territory.
Some ‘Keep Left’ signs in New South Wales, Queensland, and the Northern Territory use this thinner version, which does not include an arrow.
Termite mounds can sometimes be seen in the Northern Territory and rarely northern WA and QLD. They appear as brown, spiky formations rising out of the ground.

Queensland.text: These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland(from Gold Coast to Sunshine Coast). They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.
This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.
Bus stops in Queensland have a yellow signpost bending over the actual sign.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.
Sugarcane plantations are very common in Northern Queensland, due to its tropical climate.
Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.
Poletags with a blue sticker, and a vertical steel tag are found in Queensland, north of Rockhampton.
While Bottle Trees can be found throughout Queensland, they are planted everywhere in the city of Roma.
Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.

They are almost exclusively found between Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast
The Queensland fan palm or Australian fan palm, is a species endemic to northeastern Queensland, Australia (Specially around Cairns).
Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.

The Queensland License Plate has dark red letters which can shine through the blur. Looks similar to the NT plate, which has a lighter red tone. There is also an old, green version, which could theoretically show up.

Excoecaria parvifolia is an odd looking tree with almost creepy looking thin vine outgrowths as leaves. It seems to be found primarily found around the new 2025 white car coverage around the northern Queensland city of Gregory, Australia.

As a general rule in Queensland state, Australia, red tinted roads are found mostly around Charters Towers (especially when you have more trees), they can also be found on the A2 near label, and the 1 further north. These areas are indicated in the distribution, but there may be minor exceptions.

The landscape in inland NSW is mostly flat, and the soil gets redder the more inland you go. Vegetation consists of mostly dry pale-green shrubs. Further east and on the Queensland and Victorian borders, the climate gets more temperate but is still quite dry and more eucalyptus trees can be seen, with the soil transitioning into a more sandy colour as well as more hills being visible.

Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded. NOTE: Blue stickers can also be found on French poles.
These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.
Road signs with a fluorescent border are almost exclusively found in Queensland.

Victoria.text: You can find these white hydrant poles that feature a blue circle and a red section on top of it in Victoria.(they have couple different designs but they all follow same color/shape +/- pattern)
These fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.
According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.
Bus Stops in Victoria can be recognized by their color scheme: White-Orange-Black-Grey-White.
License plates in Victoria have a little small triangle at the top, which can sometimes be recognized through the blur.

The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint.

The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil.

In a lot of Generation 2 around the towns of Morwell and Traralgon in Eastern Victoria, an entire leaf is visible in the Generation 2 halo. A version with only the top half of a leaf can also be seen in eastern SA.

The area around Warramboo in SA to Madura in WA has a unique landscape. Vegetation is quite dry and is made up of shrubs and wide crowned eucalyptus. In addition, the soil is sandy with a slight orange tint. The dry area east of Adelaide and into northwestern Victoria has a similar landscape, with the same vegetation but usually with whiter soil. NOTE: The soil gets more red in the WA side. Redder soil can also be seen more inland on the Victorian side around Mildura. In addition, the Nullarbor Highway has a distinct landscape.

Qld.text: If you see this grayish long thin plate with numbers, sometimes with extra blue(or other color) little circle marking you gonna be in QLD(not in south east most likely because they use different marking).
The northern QLD city of Cairns is distinct due to its tropical vegetation and big green mountains around the city.
Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.
This black-and-yellow bollard is exclusive to Queensland.
Coastal northern Queensland is very tropical. Typical vegetation consists of palm trees and dark green vegetation.

Sugarcane plantations are very common in Northern Queensland, due to its tropical climate. NOTE: Sugarcane plantations can be seen as far south as northern NSW, however are most commonly found in northern Queensland. For a detailed overview, see this map.

Tasmania.text: White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.
Olive-green possum guards are only found on electricity poles in Tasmania.
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.

Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape.
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape. NOTE: Regular Australian crossbars are usually made out of wood.

Tasmania has a cool temperate climate which is uncommon in the rest of Australia and is comparable to central-southern Chile or New Zealand. Typical landscape consists of green rolling hills that can look dry in winter coverage. Eucalyptus trees can be seen on the side of roads and on hills in the distance. Rural Tasmania is also quite hilly with dense eucalyptus forests making up the landscape. NOTE: Certain areas of Victoria can look similar so make sure to look for other clues.

Australian Capital Territory.text:
Australia is home to dozens of rare Google cars, which can usually be found in natural reserves.

Most rare Google cars with snorkels are located in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The only snorkel cars outside of NSW are in the northwestern part of Wunaamin Conservation Area (northern WA) and along Lucky Bay (south coastal WA).
The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that include text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.

Vic.text: According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.
A trident-like pole top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.
Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.
You can find these white hydrant poles that feature a blue circle and a red section on top of it in Victoria.
These fire hydrants with red painted tops are unique to Victoria.

Tas.text: Olive-green possum guards are only found on electricity poles in Tasmania. NOTE: Possum guards are found all over Australia. The colour is what distinguishes them.
White directional signs can only be found in Tasmania.

ACT.text: The white ‘No Stopping’ and ‘No Parking’ signs that include text are unique to the Australian Capital Territory.

spotlight.text: Alice Springs, an isolated town in the southern part of the Northern Territory, features distinct orange rocks that can be seen in the distance or at the end of roads.

The northern QLD city of Cairns is distinct due to its tropical vegetation and big green mountains around the city. NOTE: To differentiate Cairns from other northern Queensland towns, Cairns has many high rise buildings and should feel quite urban. Divided roads are also common in downtown Cairns, and only commonly seen in Mackay further south, where it is less tropical and more flat.

Kangaroo Island in South Australia tends to have a distinct look. The vegetation mostly consists of bushes and low, stubby eucalyptus trees with puffy clusters of leaves. The orange soil colour is reminiscent of Western Australia. In addition, the island only has Generation 2 and Generation 4 coverage.
On most of the Northern Territory section of the Barkly Highway and a small part of the Queensland section, a wire can be seen on the left side of the car.
Dorat Road (23) in the Northern Territory can be easily recognized thanks to its distinct Darwin area landscape and lack of road lines.

The Sturt Highway from Wentworth to Wagga Wagga can have triple broken centre lines. NOTE: Triple broken centre lines can also be found on other major roads in NSW, such as the Gwydir Highway. However, they are most common on the Sturt Highway.

All-yellow road lines can be seen on roads around Mount Kosciuszko. In addition, a unique white truck with a snorkel, and cab guard can be found. NOTE: All yellow road lines can also be found in other alpine areas in Victoria and New South Wales, so make sure to look at the landscape and other clues.
South Australian style Stobie poles can sometimes be found in the NSW town of Broken Hill.

AT.name: Austria
AT.key_meta: Austria's bollards are white with a black top and dark red or grey reflectors, often featuring a nipple-shaped black cap and sometimes a snow pole.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Austria's bollards are white with a black top and dark red or grey reflectors, often featuring a nipple-shaped black cap and sometimes a snow pole.
metas.comparison: Slovenia’s bollards are similar but always have a white back reflector, whereas in Austria, white reflectors are rare but possible.

metas.title: Austria
metas.description: Hat - Austria, Bulgaria, Czechia, Slovakia. > those with Horizontal Crosswalk - Austria.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Austria uses white bollards, with a black top. The colour of the reflector is (dark) red or dark grey.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Slovenia and Montenegro use the same bollards, but with bright red reflectors instead of grey or dark red. Germany uses simple white bollards with grey reflectors.

metas.title: Landscape
metas.description:
Most of Austria is mountainous and covered in forests.
However, some areas in the east and northeast are much more flat and agricultural.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

general_rules.text: Vienna street signs are extremely recognizable dark blue plaques with a traditional-looking white serif font. The number at the start will indicate which district you are in (see the map). You can click the image to enlarge it.

Vienna.text: Austrian B-roads, indicated by white text inside of a blue rectangle, also follow the general trend of increasing in number from east to west. An important exception to this are roads 222-230, which are located inside the state of Vienna. You can click the image to enlarge it.
Vineyards are limited to the far eastern part of the country. You can find a very precise map here. Notably, there are a lot of vineyards close to Vienna and around Lake Neusiedl.

Vorarlberg.text: Bus stops consisting of neon-yellow poles are found in Vorarlberg.
These yellow and white stripes around poles and signposts are found in Vorarlberg.
White kilometre markers can be found in Vorarlberg as well as on a road in western Salzburg.

Salzburg.text: A large white painted square in the middle of the road can be found next to kilometre markers in Salzburg.

Burgenland.text: Green “Güterweg” signs are found in Burgenland.

Upper Austria.text: White “Güterweg” signs with a black outline are mainly found in Upper Austria.

Lower Austria.text: In Lower Austria, you may find signs with yellow and blue sign borders, corresponding to the flag of the region.

spotlight.text: Most other major cities in Austria also have their own unique street signs. NOTE: Many of the arbitrary blue ones can look similar, but the 4 listed in the graphic can be differentiated by: Vienna - District Number Vienna - District Number Salzburg - Unique Font Salzburg - Unique Font Klagenfurt - Irregular White Border Klagenfurt - Irregular White Border St Polten - Rounded White Border St Polten - Rounded White Border You can click the image to enlarge it.

Poles in Vienna and Innsbruck feature these red-and-white pieces of tape that look like the Austrian flag. They can be differentiated by the fact that the tapes in Vienna are thinner, and there are typically two on each pole.

PT.name: Portugal
PT.key_meta: Old Portuguese license plates have a yellow strip on the right side.

metas.title: License plate
metas.description: Old Portuguese license plates have a yellow strip on the right side. New plates follow the standard EU design without the yellow strip.

metas.title: Pole
metas.description: Concrete ladder poles with very tall ladder steps are common in Portugal. Each step often has a small see-through hole.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

metas.title: No hunting signs
metas.description: Hunting signs with a red and white color scheme are commonly seen in rural areas of Portugal. They can be either diamond-shaped or rectangular.

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description: Portuguese bollards are either wedge-shaped with a noticeably thin white top, or flat with a wide reflector. While most reflectors will be white, you may also find orange reflectors. These are noticeably darker than the yellow reflectors in Spain.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Side walks
metas.description: Cobblestone sidewalks made of distinctly bright stones are very common in Portugal.

metas.title: Mosaic Tiles
metas.description: Houses made of decorative mosaic tiles are somewhat common in Portugal.

metas.title: Cobblestone Sidewalks
metas.description: Similarly, cobblestone sidewalks made of distinctly bright stones are very common.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Architecture
metas.description: White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common in Portugal.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Blue / Yellow Paints
metas.description: You’ll commonly see blue or yellow lines painted around windows and doors, as well as around the edges of walls.

metas.title: Belt + Bent Knees Portugal
metas.description: White Belt: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal, Germany, Hungary. > Non-Pointed Shoes: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal. Bent knees: Portugal.

metas.title: Eucalyptus Trees
metas.description:
Eucalyptus trees are very common in Portugal.
The only other part of Europe where you’ll commonly see eucalyptus is northern Spain.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Cobblestone Roads
metas.description:
Cobblestone roads are very common in Portugal.
These will typically be made of square cobblestones arranged diagonally compared to the road direction.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: License Plates
metas.description:
Portuguese plates are long and white, with a blue strip on the left.
Most plates have a yellow strip on the right, which is unique to Portugal.
The yellow strip was discontinued in 2020, so in Generation 4 coverage you may sometimes see plates with just the blue strip.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

general_rules.text: The first three digits of Portuguese landlines make up the area codes, which are distributed as seen on the map. Phone codes not starting with a 2 are not regional, and codes starting with 29 will either be the Azores or Madeira. For a complete list of the third digits, see this page.

Coverage.text: The only islands in the Azores with car coverage are Ilha de São Miguel, Ilha Terceira and Ilha do Faial.
The only island with Generation 4 coverage is Ilha de São Miguel.

Azores.text: Shitcam coverage is found on Ilha de São Miguel and Ilha do Faial. The car seen on São Miguel has an indentation in the centre, while the one on Faial appears as a smooth surface, sometimes with an antenna visible.

Lakes.text: Ilha de São Miguel is the only island in the Azores or Madeira where you can find lakes.

Whiterockwall.text: Rock walls with a white painted concrete top are somewhat common on Ilha Terceira.

Faial.text: On Ilha do Faial, you will sometimes find traditional whitewashed rock walls with unevenly sized dark basalt stones.

2Southernchimney.text: In the Faro district in the south of Portugal you will very commonly come across decorative chimneys, which will either be round or square shaped with small spire-shaped tops. The round chimneys are a particularly strong clue.

Concreteblocks.text: Houses in northern Portugal are often made of square concrete blocks, which are commonly put together with white mortar. NOTE: Very similar architecture, but typically without the white mortar, is commonly found over the border in Galicia.

2Montado.text: Open fields sparsely populated with holm oaks (Quercus ilex) and cork oaks (Quercus suber) are very common in the southeast. These species of oaks tend to be on the smaller side, and have a Mediterranean look. While these fields will look quite dry during summer and fall, they will look much lusher during spring.

2Olives.text: Olive plantations are generally more common in the eastern half of the country, particularly in the far northeast and slight southeast. NOTE: The easiest way to tell apart the olive plantations from the oak fields from the last tip is to look at the pattern in which they’re planted. Olive plantations are typically planted in dense rows, while the oaks are planted more sparsely and not in an obvious pattern.

2Eucalyptusforest.text: Dense eucalyptus forests are mostly found in the northwest.

2Maritimepine.text: Forests, or plantations of Maritime pines (Pinus Pinaster) are very common in the northern half of Portugal. You can recognize the tree by its grey bark with red undertones, and fluffy branches that point upwards. Older trees often don’t have any branches in the bottom half of the tree. NOTE: Plantations of this pine are also common in northern Spain, particularly Galicia.

2Terracedvineyards.text: In the Douro wine region, straight east of Porto, you will commonly find steep terraced vineyards.

2Citrus.text: Citrus plantations are mostly found along the south coast.

2Azoresmadeira.text: The islands of Madeira and the Azores are found southwest and west of mainland Portugal respectively. For country streak purposes they are both counted as Portugal. Plonk It has more in-depth guides to Madeira here and a guide to the Azores here.

Bananaplantation.text: The majority of banana plantations are found in the south.

Plateau.text: The centre-west of the island is home to an elevated plateau. It can be recognized by the unusual flatness, misty coverage, and the presence of wind turbines.

Streeteastplateau.text: The road east of the plateau can be recognized by its unique mountain formations and the black-and-yellow guardrail on the side of the road.

Eastdry.text: The eastern tip of the island is very arid with little to no vegetation.

spotlight.text: A trekker going along the edge of a crater can be seen on Ilha do Faial. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback
The ER211 can be recognized by the dark pavement combined with its exposed brownish soil.
Pico Areeiro is the second highest mountain on the island, and the highest with coverage. It can be recognized by its view over most of the island, and the white radar station at the top.
The Penha d'Águia is located in northeastern Madeira, isolated on an elevated hill.
The Cristiano Ronaldo International Airport is located in eastern Madeira. The north of it is built on these numerous concrete pillars.
Cascata dos Anjos is situated in the southwest and is a popular location on the island. It is a 100-metre-high waterfall, which cascades onto the road below.
The islands of Ribeira de Janela, located in the northwest, are a famous photographer spot with their vertical, jagged shape.

These dark, sharp rock formations with an island in the background are found in Porto Moniz in the northwest. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback
The Serra da Estrela natural park can be recognised by the rocky mountainous highland landscape, often combined with yellow and black striped snow poles.
Pine forests with extremely sandy white soil can be found near the coast between the cities of Setúbal and Sines.

In the far southwest of the country you can find a flat uncultivated landscape with very limited vegetation, which typically appears quite dry. There are almost no trees nearby, and only very low bushes and grass.
Lime green street signs can be found in Porto.

BD.name: Bangladesh
BD.key_meta: The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word.

metas.title: Language
metas.description: The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word. It resembles Devanagari (Hindi) but can be recognized by the many letters with triangular shapes. Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India(but coverage there is taken with "shit cam")
from_maps: A Learnable Meta South East Asia - Beginner

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Bangladesh uses red-and-white concrete bollards throughout the whole country.
metas.comparison: NOTE: They can also be found in a square form instead of a circular form.

Western.text: Bangladesh has several distinct roof styles that create an east/west divide in the country. The west, particularly the divisions of Rajshahi, Khulna and Dhaka, is dominated by hip roofs made of sheet metal. The states of Rangpur and Chittagong tend to have mixed roofs.

Eastern.text: In the east, you will commonly see sheet metal roofs with a triangular "window" just below the ridge of the roof. The state of Sylhet will exclusively have this style, which can also be seen in Chittagong, Mymensingh, eastern Rangpur and northern Dhaka.

Tiled.text: Tiled roofs are uncommon in Bangladesh, but the ones you do see are of West Bengal origin, and are thus only found on the Indian border in the state of Khulna.

Early.text: Rice is the main agricultural crop in Bangladesh and is planted twice a year. The different rice seasons can be told apart by the height and colour of the rice and are very useful for regionguessing. Short green rice that is barely sticking out of the water is known as early growth rice. Early growth rice can be seen in the states of Khulna, Mymensingh and south of Padma River in Dhaka. NOTE: Beware that this, and the following tips, are only accurate in Generation 4 coverage.

Mid.text: Slightly taller rice, in the middle of growing, which still remains green, can be seen in the states of Rangpur, Barishal and Chittagong.

Fully.text: Fully-grown rice is characterised by being noticeably taller, as well as having a yellow or orange colour and fluffier tips - the fluffiness signifies that the rice is ripe. Fully-grown rice is mostly seen in the state of Rajshahi, but it is also present in Rangpur and Chittagong.

Harvest.text: Harvested rice can be identified by its beige or brown colour and shorter, cut down appearance. It can be seen alongside fully-grown, unharvested rice as well as freshly planted early growth rice in adjacent fields. This is most commonly seen in the states of Sylhet and southern Khulna.

Off.text: Rice fields require some rest time, so it's natural to come across some off-season barren, empty fields without rice altogether. Off-season fields are mostly seen in the state of Dhaka, north of Padma River.

Empty.text: Vast rice fields with almost nothing else in view can be seen in the border area between the states of Dhaka, Mymensingh and Sylhet.

Elevation.text: While most of Bangladesh is almost completely flat, in the eastern parts of Chittagong you may find fairly tall, forested and uncultivated hills.

Sylhet.text: A sizable east-west ridge can be seen on the Indian border from the northern parts of Sylhet and eastern Mymensingh. It is often obscured or diminished by heavy haze.

Corn.text: Corn tends to be planted in the west of Bangladesh - large and medium-sized fields can be found in Rajshahi, Rangpur, western Mymensingh and northern Khulna. Smaller patches of corn can be found in the south of Barishal, usually adjacent to other crops.

Jute.text: Jute is a tall-growing green crop which gets dried and used in the making of rugs, bags and other goods. Because of when the coverage was taken, jute can almost exclusively be found on Street View in Rangpur. In its dried state it can be found hanging off fences and drying on the roads anywhere in the country.

Rapeseed.text: Canola is a low-growing crop with yellow flowers that is used to make cooking oil. It is usually planted during the off-season for rice, making it extremely common north of Padma river in the state of Dhaka.

Tea.text: Tea production in Bangladesh is concentrated in the highlands of southern Sylhet and, rarely, Chittagong.

Fruit.text: Standalone fruit trees in Bangladesh are most commonly seen in the states of Rajshahi and Rangpur. Fruit orchards with systematically planted trees, however, are concentrated near the Indian border in both states.

Sunflower.text: Sunflower fields are found in the south of Barishal state.

Watermelon.text: Fields of watermelons can also be found in the south of Barishal.

Eucalyptus.text: Eucalyptus trees are tall trees with lush crowns and ivory-coloured trunks. In Bangladesh they are more common in the north, with Rangpur, Rajshahi and Mymensingh being the most likely states.

Blossoming.text: Blossoming trees are tied to coverage and seasonal metas in Bangladesh, and are only found in the states where coverage was taken during spring time - Khulna, Mymensingh and southern Dhaka. NOTE: Beware that this is only accurate in Generation 4 coverage.

Coastal.text: Beach Sheoaks (Casuarina equisetifolia) are thin evergreen trees with thin, long, drooping branchlets. Like the name suggests, they are mostly observed in coastal regions - along the coast of the Teknaf Peninsula and around Noakhali city in Chittagong.

Barishal.text: Similarly, Generation 4 coverage with 2023 written on the copyright labels can be found in Rangpur, Rajshahi, Khulna, Barishal, Sylhet and less commonly Chittagong. NOTE: 2024 and 2025 now make up around half of all copyright dates. These can be found all over the country.

Striped.text: Generation 3 coverage with the striped Street View car can be found mostly on yellow roads west of Dhaka.

spotlight.text: In the city of Sylhet there will often be a guard at the side of the car visible, usually holding a hayfork. Note that this only applies to Generation 3 coverage.
In the city of Barishal there can also be a guard at the side of the car visible, not to be confused with the Sylhet guard. NOTE: The same man can rarely be found elsewhere on trekker coverage.
This interesting trekker with a black cover can be found in the city of Khulna.
The trekker with red colour in the mirrors is unique to the island of Nijhum Dwip.
A scooter trekker, where mostly the left mirror and some hair is visible, can be found on Hatiya Island.
A trekker escorted by a security guard is found on Saint Martin's Island.

BE.name: Belgium
BE.key_meta: Belgian license plates should have a red tint visible through the blur because they use red text on a white license plate.

metas.title: Reddish license plates
metas.description: Belgian license plates should have a red tint visible through the blur because they use red text on a white license plate.

metas.title: Belgium Lego Man
metas.description: Horizontal Zebra stripe: Austria, Belgium, Greece, Poland, Serbia. > LEGO MAN: Belgium.

metas.title: Small Priority Signs
metas.description: Priority signs in Belgium have an orange diamond and are much smaller than in other countries.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Red License Plates
metas.description:
Licence plates in Belgium use red text.
You can recognise this distinct colour even through the blur.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: South - Gray Tone Stones
metas.description: Houses in the South of the country use a lot of stone, have gray tones and generally look more French.

metas.title: Double Gutters
metas.description:
Almost all roads (big or small) in Belgium use gutters on both sides.
This is much less common in neighbouring countries.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Additional Blue Signs
metas.description:
Road signs often have an additional small blue sign.
In other European countries, these small signs are usually just white.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Belgium uses white bollards with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front and white on the back. A second type of bollard is dark brown with two red stripes at the top. Occasionally, other bollards can be seen.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Denmark uses similar white bollards, but they have a red stripe at the top and the reflector is not rectangular. The dark brown bollard with two red stripes can also be seen in the Netherlands.

general_rules.text: Phone codes in Belgium are very useful to determine the region you are in. They are 9 digits long. The 1 or 2 number(s) after the leading 0 indicate the area code. 0X XXX XX XX (Brussels, Antwerp, Liege, Ghent.) 0XX XX XX XX (Other cities.) NOTE: Mobile numbers start with 04 and are 10 digits long. You can click on the image to enlarge it.

Wallonia.text: Belgium has 3 official languages. Dutch (Flemish), spoken in Flanders, the Northern part of Belgium. There is an abundance of letters and combinations like z, w, ee and ij. Dutch (Flemish), spoken in Flanders, the Northern part of Belgium. There is an abundance of letters and combinations like z, w, ee and ij. French (Walloon), spoken in Wallonia, the Southern part of Belgium. You can see letters like ç, é, è and à. French (Walloon), spoken in Wallonia, the Southern part of Belgium. You can see letters like ç, é, è and à. German, spoken in Ostbelgien, a small region in the east of the country. You can see letters like ä, ü, ö and ß. German, spoken in Ostbelgien, a small region in the east of the country. You can see letters like ä, ü, ö and ß.
Bus stop signs in Flanders (and Brussels) have a white rectangle at the top. In Wallonia they will have a yellow top.

In Flanders (and Brussels), 95% of warning signs have a thick red outline, without a white border. Contrarily, you will most often find warning signs with a small white outline in Wallonia. NOTE: The signs found in Flanders are the same as the Spanish ones.
Traffic lights held up by yellow-and-black poles are unique to Flanders. In contrast, Wallonia and Brussels frequently use a red-and-white design.

Brussels.text: Brussels, the capital of Belgium, is bilingual. You will see both French and Dutch on signs.

Luxembourg.text: The Ardennes, located in the southeast part of Belgium, have a very distinct landscape. You can see a lot of steep hills, dense forests, and valleys. NOTE: The Ardennes extend partially into France, Luxembourg, and Germany.

Antwerp.text: The coastal plain is extremely flat and consists of so-called polders, which are man-made fields at or below sea level, surrounded by many waterways. This landscape is situated near the North Sea coast, as well as near the western part of the border with the Netherlands, particularly around Antwerp. NOTE: This part of Belgium is especially often confused with the Netherlands. Carefully look around for clues to distinguish the two countries if you find yourself in this landscape.

spotlight.text: Baarle-Hertog, located north-east of Antwerp, is composed of several exclaves and enclaves of Belgium and the Netherlands. You can often see the country's borders in this city (indicated by small white crosses). Street name signs tell you whether you are in Belgium or The Netherlands.

BM.name: Bermuda
BM.key_meta: If you see a black Street View car with the entire front side of the vehicle visible, you're in Bermuda.

metas.title: Unique car
metas.description: If you see a black Street View car with the entire front side of the vehicle visible, you're in Bermuda.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta World - Google Cars - Beginner

metas.title: White Roofs
metas.description:
Most buildings on Bermuda are single family stone houses painted in pastel colours.
They will almost always have completely white roofs.

metas.title: Hamilton
metas.description: Hamilton is by far the largest town on Bermuda, and as such, the downtown area is distinct due to its many large, densely built multi-floor buildings.

Downtownhamilton.text: Hamilton is by far the largest town on Bermuda, and as such, the downtown area is distinct due to its many large, densely built multi-floor buildings.

spotlight.text: The northwestern tip of Bermuda can be recognised by the many large buildings made of unpainted grey brick.
A boat trekker can be seen on the eastern coast of Bermuda. It can be seen going around Saint George’s Harbour and past Fort St. Catherine on the northeast tip of the island.

BT.name: Bhutan
BT.key_meta: License plates in Bhutan are almost always red and are easily visible on vehicles.

metas.title: Red license plate
metas.description: License plates in Bhutan are almost always red and are easily visible on vehicles.

metas.title: Architecture
metas.description: Traditional Bhutanese architecture is very distinct. Most houses feature tin roofs and wooden painted frames, giving them a unique look.

metas.title: Stone blocks guardrail
metas.description: Bhutan commonly uses stone blocks as safety barriers on winding rural roads. These blocks are very common and are one of the best ways to recognize rural roads in Bhutan.

metas.title: Unique Architecture
metas.description:
The traditional Bhutanese architecture is very distinct.
Most of the houses have tin roofs and wooden painted frames, which give them a unique look.

Coverage.text: Most of the Bhutanese street view coverage was taken on the main roads and cities.

Landscape.text: Flat landscapes like this in Bhutan can only be found in the south. NOTE: The coverage in the south is limited to the four regions shown on the map.

Probjihkavalley.text: The Phobjikha Valley, south of Nubding, is a wide and relatively flat agricultural valley. It is by far the largest open valley with no major river visible on Street View.

spotlight.text: A hook can be seen on the back of the car in Haa District, mainly in the town of Ha. NOTE: The hook is sometimes just barely visible due to the car blur.
Late sunset coverage can be found in two places in the country; on a small rural sideroad in the east of Mongar District and in a significantly more urban area around the town of Paro in the west.
Gelephu Airport is the only airport located in the flat south part of Bhutan, making it recognisable.
The Paro International Airport is located in a dry northwest valley and is one of the two northern airports.
While the Paro International Airport is located in a dry northwest valley, the Bumthang Domestic Airport is located in a wet northern valley.

BO.name: Bolivia
BO.key_meta: Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia are noticeably curvy and appear to be made from locally sourced tree trunks.

metas.title: Curvy poles
metas.description: Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia are noticeably curvy and appear to be made from locally sourced tree trunks.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

Coveragemap.text: Coverage in Bolivia is very limited, both in geographic scope and the density of roads covered. Only the central and central-western parts of the country have coverage. Most coverage is found in and around the six main cities of La Paz or El Alto, Cochabamba, Oruro, Sucre, Potosi, and Santa Cruz. These aforementioned six cities have in-depth side-street coverage. Outside these cities, coverage is mostly limited to main roads. Beware that “main road” is a relative concept in Bolivia: many of these, even some that are marked yellow on the map, have large unpaved sections.

Altiplano.text: The Altiplano (“high plain”) is an immense highland plateau that dominates most of western Bolivia. It is covered in grasslands that range from green to arid. Some parts are suitable for agriculture, whereas other parts are extremely dry. Grass growing in tufts is common (sometimes referred to as “Bolivian hedgehogs” in the community). NOTE: While it is generally fairly flat, you will often see hills and mountains around you. However, as a general rule, the road itself will be mostly flat.

Greenaltiplano.text: The grasslands of the Altiplano tend to look more lush in the more northern half: the area close to El Alto and La Paz. NOTE: Due to seasonal coverage, there are some exceptions to this, but in general this is a good rule of thumb to distinguish between the different parts of the Altiplano.

Aridaltiplano.text: Conversely, the Altiplano looks more arid in the more southern half: around Oruro, and the roads going southwest towards Chile. NOTE: There is one major exception to this: one driving side of the divided part of Ruta 1 looks somewhat green all the way up to Oruro (due to this coverage being captured in a different season).

Laketiticaca.text: Lake Titicaca, on the border with Peru, is the most significant body of water in Bolivia. It is located entirely within the Altiplano. It can be seen from two roads: The section of Ruta 1 between Desaguadero and Guaqui. Here, the lake will always be to your north. The section of Ruta 1 between Desaguadero and Guaqui. Here, the lake will always be to your north. The section of Ruta 2 between San Pablo de Tiquina and Batallas. Here, the lake will mostly be to your south or west. The section of Ruta 2 between San Pablo de Tiquina and Batallas. Here, the lake will mostly be to your south or west. The landscape around Titicaca is very green, compared to most of the western half of Bolivia.

Mountains.text: If you are surrounded by tall mountains, you are likely in the Andes, which goes roughly northwest to southeast in between the Altiplano and the Amazon rainforest. NOTE: The Altiplano has several smaller and solitary mountains.

Eastofandes.text: The area east of the Andes is very green and tropical, with lots of agriculture – especially around Santa Cruz. This area is mostly very flat, though you will see large hills on some of the roads closer to the Andes. The soil tends to have a pink colour.

Santacruzunpaved.text: Within this tropical area, coverage on unpaved roads is only found around Santa Cruz. These roads again prominently have the pink soil that is very characteristic of the area east of Andes.

Cobblestone.text: Aside from being a useful identifier for the country, cobblestone roads are mainly found in and southeast of Cochabamba. They also appear around Sucre and, very rarely, in La Paz.

BW.name: Botswana
BW.key_meta: Botswana has many unique and distinct regions throughout the country.

metas.title: Vibes
metas.description:
A dry, flat landscape with African vegetation, usually a bit away from the road, is a good clue for Botswana and becomes quite distinct after seeing it couple times.
You can confirm it's Botswana by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north.
metas.comparison: The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

general_rules.text: Botswana has many unique and distinct regions throughout the country. This image breaks down the main factors that differentiate each distinctive landscape by soil, vegetation and other clues. You can click on the image to enlarge it. RESOURCE: This image was made possible by the invaluable research done by Jasper Woodard. You can check out his Botswana videos on his YouTube channel.

Coverage.text: Coverage in Botswana is fairly limited due to the country’s sparse road system. In addition to regular paved roads, you can still expect to see some rural unpaved road coverage. The most dense coverage is in the east and near Gaborone. The larger towns have extensive side road coverage.

Small.text: This map shows which covered roads are paved, and which ones are unpaved. It is slightly simplified for ease of reading. Small, unpaved side roads in and near towns are not shown.

Elevation.text: Most of Botswana is as flat as a pancake. However, every now and then you will find some elevation. If you see hills, you are most likely in one of the two areas indicated on the minimap. NOTE: Even in the indicated areas, there are a lot of very flat areas, as many of Botswana’s hills are geographically isolated. Some lone hills may also appear far outside the indicated areas.

Bots.text: The southeastern region near Gaborone has many semi-arid hills covered in short shrubs. If you see a lot of these, you are likely to be in the area between Gaborone and Lobatse. NOTE: Similar hills can be found elsewhere in the country and across the border in South Africa. If you see a large quantity of them, and use other clues to rule out South Africa, you can be fairly certain that you are in southeastern Botswana.

Eastern.text: The landscape in the eastern pocket north of Francistown is characterised by red soil and a somewhat arid look. The soil in these two areas often looks firm and rocky, rather than sandy or dusty. Trees and bushes with yellowed leaves and other “autumn” colours are common. Many trees are bare and withered. You might see fallen leaves on the ground here and there.

Sand.text: A large region in the middle western part of the country is characterised by very white sandy soil. In addition, the vegetation tends to look very dry. NOTE: Sandy soil can be found in many places in Botswana. This tip specifically refers to the bright white colour of the sand.

A35.text: The A35 is a very recognisable road: there is always a power line to your west. It can also be recognised by its grainy asphalt with faded markings. Many small tracks can be found parallel to the road, disappearing into the bushes.

A33.text: The A33 is characterised by a landscape that is more lush than usual. Trees have lots of green leaves and the grass is very tall. The more north you go, the more lush the vegetation becomes.

Middlepits.text: The road that runs along Botswana’s southern border, through the town of Middlepits, has asphalt with a distinct red tint. The landscape is arid. In some sections, slight hills can be seen. NOTE: Near the town of Middlepits itself, the soil is very red and dotted with small white pebbles.

Gaborone.text: Gaborone is the capital and largest city. It tends to look richer and more developed than the rest of Botswana, though some neighbourhoods may still look impoverished. In some southern parts of the city hills can be seen, but most of the town is flat. NOTE: The only other place in the country that often looks similar is Francistown.

Francistown.text: In Francistown, you can often see a lone hill with radio antennas, which is located on the north side of the city. This hill is a good way to distinguish Francistown from Gaborone. NOTE: The town of Serowe has a similar hill with antennas. Here, the towers are taller, red-and-white striped, and the hill has a flat top.

Maun.text: Maun is the only relatively large city in Botswana that has this bright white sandy soil, which is typical for the middle western region of the country.

spotlight.text: The western part of the A2 has overcast coverage, making it recognisable.

Chobe Flood Plains National Park in the far north has a lot of small, winding dirt road coverage, with a lot of it being just south of the Chobe River. It has scattered lush bushes on either side, and you will often find wildlife such as elephants and warthogs.

This portion of the A30 has a distinct autumn feel unique to it. Notably, there are trees with orange coloured leaves lining the road in straight rows. In addition, there is often tall grass as opposed to other autumn looking locations.

Salt pans can be found in central-eastern Botswana. Dirt road coverage can be found leading to the pans and has similar soil and grass, but you can also find many trees along the road. They are mainly found around the Nwetwe pan. The salt pans show up as lakes on the map. NOTE: A lot of the dirt road coverage near the pans was taken in June, and will feature trees without leaves or those that are beginning to lose their leaves.

Just outside Gaborone, there is a lot of coverage along very rural, small dirt tracks. They can be identified by the orange-red shade of dirt and abundance of green trees and bushes surrounding the road.

The section of the A33 within the Sibuya Forest Reserve and the CT/3 (Tamafupa) Commercial Wildlife Utilisation is under construction. This is most visible by the service road or embankment alongside the road. NOTE: Despite being in the construction zone, some locations may still look normal.

The mostly unpaved road north of Maun to Khwai can be identified by extremely white sandy soil and tall green trees surrounding the road. The first section of the road, between Maun and Shorobe, is paved. But that section can still be identified by the trees, faint road markings, and power lines to the west of the road.
The A20 has mostly clean, recent asphalt. Some sections of the road are much thinner than usual. The landscape is characterised by red soil, dry grey-coloured trees, and very little grass.

Southeast of Tshabong, the A20 has been recently repainted and has very bright yellow lines and relatively dark asphalt. There is a powerline running alongside it to the northeast, it has orange-tan sandy soil, and you can often find patches of yellow flowers.
The Tsodilo Hills World Heritage Site is memorable due to its large protruding hills with exposed rock faces. The coverage around the hills is entirely on dirt roads.
These distinctive silos are found in Pandamatenga in northeastern Botswana and can be seen all around the town.

metas.title: Pole
metas.description: The most common poles in Brazil resemble a ladder at the bottom. They are rectangular, with long segments at the base and small holes near the top. Chilean poles look similar but have 1–2 larger sections at the bottom instead of 3+ like Brazilian poles.
metas.comparison: You might also find rounded concrete or wooden poles in Brazil, but they are less common and can be used for region-guessing within the country.

metas.title: Landscape - Landbridge in Rio Grande do Sul
