metas.title: Infrastructure - Campinas Sidewalk
metas.description: The city of Campinas, SP is known for it's unique and artistic patterns of black and white stones on its sidewalks.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Umuarama
metas.description: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific, uniquely shaped one is unique to the town of Umuarama.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Parana Black Square
metas.description: This tiny black paint is rarely found on larger poles in Paraná. Still worth a quick scan, especially in urban locs.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Pole-Attached Sign
metas.description: Some poles in Curitiba, PR have street signs attached to them. Curitiba still uses regular, generic street signs, though.

metas.title: Landscape - Swampy Road
metas.description: A very swampy road (PA-154) can be found Northwest of Belém. Notably, there are very few trees, and the soil is very red.

metas.title: Infrastructure - BR-101 in the Northeast
metas.description: This road is divided. What makes it special is that one direction as asphalt and the other direction has concrete pavement.
metas.comparison: This does not apply to the entire road anymore

metas.title: Infrastructure - WiFi-Password Pole-ID
metas.description: If you find pole IDs with codes that resemble WiFi-passwords (mix of digits, upper- and lowercase letters), you're in Curitiba, PR.

metas.title: Landscape - BR174 in Amazonas
metas.description: This road can be recognized by the Amazonian looking trees and the NW/SE angle. It always has Gen 4 and an exposed, blue car front.

metas.title: Infrastructure - MA006
metas.description: Most of this road has a thick (1m) stripe of red dirt on the sides of the road. The road is oriented North-South and frequently shows Babassu palms

metas.title: Landscape - BR319, North of Porto Velho
metas.description: This road is characterized by it's Amazonian look and the SW-NE road angle. Some sections of this road are overcast and/or showcase a flat landscape.

metas.title: Landscape - BR230 in Amazonas
metas.description: This wide dirt road has Amazonian trees and a blurred car. You will not find other cars on the road. It's the only East-to-West angle road in that area.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Loanda
metas.description: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with a plain white lamp and no painted patterns on it - is unique to the town of Loanda.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Round Pole
metas.description: Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

metas.title: Landscape - Uneven Stone + Corn
metas.description: This beautiful road west of Cascavel and South of Toledo, by the PR-585 is characterized by the uneven red stone pavement and the corn plantation next to it.

metas.title: Landscape - BR230 in Para
metas.description: This road looks like an Amazonian road with the trees and dense rainforest. It runs east-west, slightly to the south. The road looks like its stained with mud

metas.title: Infrastructure - Small Red Tactile Pavement
metas.description: Small tile, circular bumps, red tactile pavement is very common in Vitoria, ES. (Do not confuse with Florianopolis, which has large tile red tactile pavement).

metas.title: Infrastructure - Surprising Wooden Pole
metas.description: In Porto Alegre, there is noticeably more foliage, cleaner, and more spacious than any other city which makes the common wooden poles look somewhat out of place.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Uberaba ID
metas.description: In Uberaba, pole IDs start with 2 or 3, and sometimes with 1. In Belo Horizonte, meanwhile, they start with 0 or 1. They do not appear in any other cities in MG.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Londrina Black Pole ID
metas.description: These black pole IDs are common in the state of Paraná, except for the capital Curitiba. If the black pole has a decimal marker (.) in the number, it's in Londrina.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Amapa Blur
metas.description: In all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá, the front right of the camera is smudged. In addition, all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features the white car with the blue stripe.

metas.title: Vegetation - Coconut Palm
metas.description: Coconut palm trees have long leaves, can grow very tall, and have thin trunks. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.

metas.title: Vegetation - Babassu Palm
metas.description: Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.

metas.title: Trekker - Amazonian Trekker
metas.description: This Amazonian trekker combines boat and walking coverage on and near the Madeira and Aripuana rivers, south of the 319. They are seen travelling through dense rainforest and small villages.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Goioere
metas.description: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with the yellow support - is unique to the town of Goioere. However, in newer coverage, the yellow supports are rarer to find.

metas.title: Landscape - Amazon Rainforest
metas.description: The Amazon is a dense rainforest that compromises 40% of Brazil's total area. Not many roads are within it, but those that are, mostly go through either biodiverse forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.

metas.title: Vegetation - Acai Palm
metas.description: Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the leaflets droop downward along with their unusually thin trunks.
metas.comparison: Note by MB: They are very similar to the Jucara Palm (which grows in Southern Brazil). Tips for differentiation:

metas.title: Trekker - Lençóis Maranhenses National Park
metas.description: The beautiful National Park of Northeast Maranhão, known for its sand dunes with pools of water, has walking trekker and vehicle coverage. The truck is white with a black bed. The landscape can vary from beach to sandy wetland.

metas.title: Landscape - BR-163 in Para
metas.description: The Pará section of the 163 is often hilly, curvy, dry, and sometimes hazy. It has a wide range of amazonian vegetation. The road is frequently trafficked, usually by transportation trucks. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

metas.title: Vegetation - Acrocomia Totai (Paraguay Palm)
metas.description: This palm is commonly mistaken to be a Macaw Palm (Acrocomia Aculeata). The key difference is that the trunk of the "Paraguay Palm" is often smoother and less irregular. The crown can also give some hints although it's difficult to catch the differences
metas.comparison: The distribution is also a bit different, as this palm usually is closer to Paraguay than the Macaw Palm which stretches further.

general_rules.text: Area codes are common to see in Brazil. They are often notated using parentheses, or at minimum as two separate numbers. Phone numbers are sometimes without area codes, and without them will be 8 numbers long for landline and 9 for mobile. The pattern for each of the states is very learnable and useful. The area codes are grouped by first digit, so even just learning those can already help a lot. Notably, area codes ending in 1 will always be around major cities and state capitals.

Postcodes (CEP) are seen frequently on street signs in Brazil (though sometimes hard to read). The first two numbers will depict an area, a state or multiple states. The numbers go anti-clockwise from São Paulo, ending in Rio Grande do Sul.

Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.
Phone numbers can sometimes be seen underneath kilometre markers in São Paulo.

Lamps in Belo Horizonte and Uberaba in Generation 4 can have a white, numbered plaque attached to the lamp. In Belo Horizonte, the tag starts with 0 or 1, and in Uberaba, it starts with a 1 or 2. Since this plaque is new, it may appear in other cities in Minas Gerais in the future.

Rio Grande do Sul.text: These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.
Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and in Rio Grande do Sul.
Northwest Rio Grande do Sul has coverage with this camera glitch in Generation 3.
Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.
These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Coastal regions in Rio Grande do Sul are recognisable due to being a rare flat wetland, which is uncommon in Brazil.
Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
The landscape in Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat with lush, green fields. Southern areas can have some resemblance to Uruguay.
These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.
You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.
Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

Transparent, mushroom-shaped insulators are common in Alagoas.
They less frequently appear in Coastal Santa Catarina.
Rarely, they also appear in coastal Rio Grande do Sul, coastal Sao Paulo and in Sergipe.

Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This is because metal signs are expensive. This is also possible on Northern Rio Grande do Sul ladder poles. An exception is the town of Sinop, Mato Grosso.

Closely related to the Açaí palm, they are really hard to distinguish apart from each other. However, the Açaí palm grows mostly in the northern flat regions of Brazil, while the Juçara grows in the mountainous south-east regions of Brazil anywhere from Espirito Santo down to Rio Grande do Sul.

Here some tips for differences:
The landscape in Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat with lush, green fields. Southern areas can have some resemblance to Uruguay.

These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.
These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and in Rio Grande do Sul.
Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.

These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too. NOTE: The same roads are seen in the Misiones province of Argentina.
You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.
Coastal regions in Rio Grande do Sul are recognisable due to being a rare flat wetland, which is uncommon in Brazil.

Ceara.text: This asymmetrical concrete crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara.
Lamps in Ceará often have a fancy and colourful arm, whether as lampposts or attached to utility poles. It sometimes says the town on the arm.

Rio de Janeiro.text: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.
When there is something out of the ordinary happening with the pole, it's Rio de Janeiro.
This yellow polepaint, similar to Sao Paulo, but with all numbers, can be found in Rio de Janeiro.

Most commonly found in Paraiba in the North, and in Parana, Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.
It's pretty rare.

Memorize the distribution map for more details. Note by MB: They're also different to the lollipop insulator, where the ridges have different sizes.
This road can be found North of Rio de Janeiro (city). It is a concrete road with black tar behind the road lines.
These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.

Gamma pole with an electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Most common in Belem, Salvador and Rio de Janeiro. Can appear occasionally in Ceara and Alagoas.

In RJ, they are particularly common in Sao Goncalo, but appear statewide.
Short crossbeam, support bar and electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Only found in Belem. (unlike the regular Gamma pole with box which can also be found in Salvador and Rio de Janeiro).

Queen palms have leaf stems that point upwards on the trunk and then "bow down" again to the ground due to gravity. They are native to South America. In Brazil, they are mainly found along the coast between Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre.

Outside of South America, they're also found in Florida and East Coast Queensland.

This map west of the city of Rio de Janeiro is unique due to the water in the south, the roadlines (double yellow - double broken yellow - single broken white) and the little wall in the North. Rio mountains can be seen in most sections of the road to the North.
Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.
Poles that have a smooth cone on top, often called a pencil pole, are common in the state of Rio de Janeiro and rarely in Brasília and Manaus.

Gamma-shaped poles containing electricity boxes at the end of the bar are most commonly seen in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the cities of Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió. NOTE: A variation with a shorter bar is exclusive to Belém.
These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.
Lamps in Rio de Janeiro are curved through the whole of the lamp arm, which is not seen anywhere else.

Minas Gerais.text: Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.
Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.
This rather large pole ID is common in Betim, Minas Gerais.
These pole IDs are specific for Minas Gerais. If they start with 0 or 1, it's Belo Horizonte.

73% of Cotton Production in Brazil takes place in Mato Grosso.
20% take place in the western border of Bahia.
Other minor spots are western Minas Gerais, Southern Goias and Northern MGDS

Acre.text: Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.
Wooden houses on stilts are very common in the state of Acre.

The 364 through Acre is very recognisable due to the rollercoaster-like landscape and road: the road uniquely rides the hills rather than snaking around them. There is usually no traffic, and is covered mostly by Generation 3 with an antenna.

Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.

Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.
Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.
Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.

Pernambuco.text: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of São Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.

Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.
Pernambuco sometimes uses these brown mushroom insulators.
This ID with two sections, the upper one being a square with a number in it, appears in Pernambuco.
Yellow plate attached by zip tie or metal strip. If it is higher up on the pole, it's in Pernambuco.
Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of Sao Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.
The Goias pole ID uses yellow paint with black numbers or a black plate with yellow numbers. Unlike the Bahia and Pernambuco IDs, the ID consists exclusively of digits.
Yellow paint with black numbers, starts with a letter. Possible in Bahia and Pernambuco. The letter is often specific to a town. Goias uses similar paint IDs, but they consist only of digits.

These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.
Insulators that resemble brown mushrooms are only found in Pernambuco.

These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.

Rio Grande do Norte.text: Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

They're found almost anywhere, but can still resolve some 50/50s:

They are only rarely found in Rio Grande do Norte. Also they're less common in Pernambuco, Parana, Santa Catarina.
Flooded coverage can be found between Macau and Macauzinho in Rio Grande do Norte.
Outer Dashed Lines can rarely be found in Rio Grande do Norte or other northeast states.

2-part lamp, most commonly seen in Minas Gerais and Goias. This particular variant with a the pole visible underneath is more common in Goias.

Otherwise, this pole appears in Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul (very useful if you have North/South vibe), spill in Distrito Federal and extremely rarely in Para, Mato Grosso and Rondonia.
Crossbars with no support bars are almost exclusively found in Piaui, Ceara, Rio Grande do Norte and Alagoas. They also frequently appear in the North-East in general, and in Rondonia and Roraima.

This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.

Electricity company names in Brazil are commonly engraved onto the poles, with their names sometimes corresponding to state names. For example, CELPA stands for Para, COSERN for Rio Grande do Norte or COELCE for Ceara.

The vast majority of poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached to the pole, as opposed to it being attached with a plate, which is much more common generally.
Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.

This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.

Long grey insulators, not including when they are horizontal, are most commonly found in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná and Santa Catarina. They are found rarely in Maranhão, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe, Rondônia, and Rio Grande do Sul. Other states have between 0 and 5%.
Lamps in Minas Gerais and Goias will often feature two parts to them. They can also be found in Rio Grande do Norte, Ceará, Rio Grande do Sul as well as the Federal District.

The vast majority of poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached to the pole, as opposed to it being attached with a plate, which is much more common generally.

Roraima.text: Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.
This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.

Lamps in Roraima have a similar style but have different colours in the main cities. Boa Vista, Normandia, and Mucajaí have red lamps, Rorainópolis has blue lamps, Pacaraima and Iracema have green, and Caracaraí has yellow.

This very unique looking road features rolling hills, which is unusual for the rather flat Roraima. It is a windy dirt road and despite being green, it lacks trees. What seperates this from the road south of Uiramuta is that it's more skinny and steeper.

Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.
This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.

Lamps in Roraima have a similar style but have different colours in the main cities. Boa Vista, Normandia, and Mucajaí have red lamps, Rorainópolis has blue lamps, Pacaraima and Iracema have green, and Caracaraí has yellow.
The landscape near the town of Uiramuta, in northern Roraima, features a very distinct landscape. It is dry, with large mountains containing numerous “folds.”

Mato Grosso do Sul.text: Macaw palms have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

This one is basically a sub-category of the 6+ Ridge Insulator. It's common in Para, Parana, Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.

However, it's not always easy to tell apart, but the longer the insulator feels, the more you should consider those states.

Assymetrical crossbeam and insulator position with a long support bar reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbeam.

Extremely common in Sao Paulo, common in Rio Grande do Sul. Less common Rio de Janeiro, Espirito Santo and Mato Grosso do Sul (where it appears most oftenly in Tres Lagoas). Rare in Mato Grosso.

Macaw palms, often called Paraguay palms, have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

This poletop, consisting of an asymmetrical crossbar and a support reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbar, is the most common poletop in the state of São Paulo. It can also be frequently seen in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.

Insulators that resemble white mushrooms are found in Bahia and rarely Brasília.

Neon-yellow, vertical IDs can be found in Campo Grande, MS and Vitoria, ES. Do not confuse with horizontal neon-yellow IDs (Sao Paulo)

Small, blue, hanging from the lamp arm.
Found in Cuiaba (bend attached to pole), and in the cities of Riberao Preto and Sao Paulo (normal lamp arm)

This long blue lamp with a top light and a unique pattern on the underside is specific to Tocantins.

Piaui.text: A road with a thin, red stripe out of gravel can be found east of Teresina, Piaui.

Mato Grosso.text:
Big electricity counters on the pole are most common in Mato Grosso, Para and Amapa.

Unlike their smaller version, they do not appear in Paraiba.

An electricity counter with a compact design can be seen in Mato Grosso, Para, Amapa and Paraiba.

The "less compact" variant with several counters does not exist in Paraiba.
Soybeans appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.

Para.text: Open or trashed electric boxes appear frequently in Maraba and Santarém (both Para).
Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

Paraiba.text: This ID is uncommon, but unique to Paraiba (most common in the capital Joao Pessoa).
The road between Caico, RGDN and Santa Luzia, Paraiba is unique with its post bushfire coverage. The part in Paraiba often has outer dashed lines

Parana.text:
Serra do Mar is a high mountain range that runs close to the coast from Parana to Northern RGDS.

If you have a high altitude road going on the mountains, instead of in the valleys, you're likely here.
A tiny black pole paint, containing a white number with a triangle-shaped arrow. Unique to Cascavel, Parana.
Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.
Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This can sometimes extend to Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul if there are ladder poles in the city.

Santa Catarina.text: Poles on Florianopolis, especially on Santa Catarina Island are painted white with blue and red stripes.
Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles can be found across Brazil, but they are more common in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
Buildings in the southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, can be of European influence (typically vaguely German) in design and style.

This road in eastern Santa Catarina is characterized by its windyness and by the steep mountains and cliffs along its side. It can feel like your driving with the clouds. The road goes through Corvo Branco which is a famous tourist attraction.
Transparent insulators are mostly in Alagoas in the northeast, and Santa Catarina in the south. They can be seen rarely in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.
Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles can be found across Brazil, but they are more common in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
Poles on Santa Catarina Island (Florianópolis) are painted white with blue and red stripes.

Amazonas.text: Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape. They are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima, but can be found in all of the Amazonian states.

The Amazonas 319 has a very lush, bright green and tropical landscape, as it cuts through the Amazon rainforest. The road is flat and mostly unpaved, featuring bright orange soil. However, closer to Manaus the road becomes paved. There are wooden or ladder poles alongside the entire stretch. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape. They are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima, but can be found in all of the Amazonian states. NOTE: These palms can additionally be found very commonly in the Amazonian parts of Colombia and Peru.

Distrito Federal.text: This little hat on the top, which makes the whole pole resemble a pencil, is most common in Rio de Janeiro, but can also be found in Manaus and Distrito Federal.

Amapa.text: This road is characterized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front of a blue-striped car), the red, and the road angle to Northwest. There are frequently Areca palms growing near this road.

This part of the BR156 can be recognized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front right of the blue-striped car). It's the only Amapa Blur coverage on a road that goes East-West. This part of the road is paved.

Eucalyptus Grandis, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations, as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapa too.

Rondonia.text: This asymmetrical crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia. NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the Rondonian variation features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.

general_rules.text: Area codes in Bulgaria are one of the best clues to regionguess urban rounds. Conveniently, they are ordered by first digit, so just learning the first digit can yield high results with little effort. Numbers between parentheses in the map are area codes from a neighbouring province that frequently spill into that one. Codes next to a small dot represent area codes unique to the province capital.

Topographic.text: The Balkan mountains cut across Bulgaria and divide the country in two distinct halves. North of them, you will find a mostly flat area that goes all the way to the border with Romania. The Rhodope Mountains start close to Sofia and run South-East into Greece. In them you will find the highest peaks of Bulgaria. Between both mountain ranges you will find the second biggest flat area of Bulgaria. The westernmost part of the country usually features many small valleys surrounded by hills and small mountains.

National.text: The towering mountains of Pirin and Rila National Parks can be recognised by the tall pyramid-shaped peaks, and can be seen from a few different vantage points in Blagoevgrad, Kyustendil and Sofia Provinces.

Wind.text: Wind turbines are most common in Dobrich Province, and usually towards the coast.

Alpine.text: Buildings with features similar to Alpine architecture, such as white walls with brown wooden details are commonly found in and around the Smoljan region in the south.

Invisible.text: Locations with an invisible Generation 4 Street View car can be found along the North and West borders of Bulgaria, as well as the northern half of the coast.

With.text: A red Generation 4 Street View car is mostly found in central and southeastern Bulgaria. This car can be found with and without an antenna.

Tape.text: Generation 3 coverage with a piece of tape on a short antenna can be commonly found in the eastern part of Bulgaria. NOTE: Tape antennas can very rarely appear in other provinces, the only provinces where it’s never found are Vratsa, Montana, Pazardzhik and Smolyan.

Long.text: Generation 3 locations with a taped long antenna and visible white car can be found in Stara Zagora, and rarely a few small roads in Plovdiv and Burgas. NOTE: This combination of car and antenna can be found more commonly in other European countries as well. Make sure to use other clues.

Varna.text: This antenna with unpeeled tape at the top, resulting in a bulkier antenna tip, can be found in the Varna Province. Coverage with this antenna is exclusively in March, resulting in a dead winter look.

spotlight.text: The mountains overlooking Vratsa from the southwest have a very distinct “bumpy” shape, and can be seen from afar in the province.

The old town of Nessebar, and to a lesser extent Sozopol, can be recognised by the well-preserved old buildings made of a combination of unpainted stone, white stone walls and brown wood. Most of the streets are paved with cobblestone.
White street signs with two red strips; one covering the bottom and one covering part of the top, can be found in Sofia. NOTE: You can also find other types of street signs in Sofia.
Brown street signs with bright yellow text can be found in Stara Zagora.

Coverage.text: Street view coverage is somewhat limited. Most of the coverage is located around the cities of Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and Battambang. You can click on the image to enlarge it. You can also view the official street view coverage in more detail on this site.

Agriculture.text: The low-lying central plain is home to most agricultural land. The landscape is flat, cultivated, and dotted with villages and farms.

Northeast.text: Conversely, the northeast is much more uncultivated: there is less agriculture and more natural vegetation. Some areas are slightly hilly.

Mountains.text: The southwest is the area with the most elevation in Cambodia. This region is characterized by hills and low mountains. Some inland roads feature dense forest cover, but the coastal areas in particular are fairly densely populated.

Sandy.text: Sandy, white soil is very common in the region southeast of Phnom Penh, as well as around the city itself. The colour can range from bright white to slightly beige. NOTE: You may find sandy, white soil in other parts of the country, however it is by far the most common in this area. Conversely, some roads in this region can have darker soil than expected.

Thai.text: Near the northern border with Thailand, you can often see a mountainous ridgeline to your north. The soil in this region tends to be red, ranging from a slight reddish tinge to deep dark red. The ridgeline closely corresponds with the border with Thailand. The drop-off to the Cambodian lowland to its south is abrupt. This means that the roads you are on are themselves located in a very flat landscape (see inset map).

spotlight.text: Black-and-white bollards in Cambodia are only found on Road 48, between Tatai and the intersection with Road 4. NOTE: Make sure to check other clues before guessing, because this style of bollard is commonly found in Thailand.
The road between Road 48 and Kiri Sakor is under construction and only has one paved road side. The unpaved side has red soil.

Several unpaved jungle offroads in the southwest of the country, northeast of Road 48, have a distinct look: red soil, dense jungle, and generally hilly terrain. NOTE: Some rural jungle roads in the east of the country can look similar. Here, however, the soil tends to be more brownish or orange rather than red.

The coverage close to Phnum Samkos has a distinct look: overcast weather, and large, prominent mountains that are visible in the distance. The roads are unpaved and consist of brown soil. Wild, very green vegetation can be seen all around you.

Unique triangular bollards with red stripes can be found in three places in Cambodia, all located in the same area in the southwest: On Road 4 between Angk Snuol and Preah Sihanouk. They are especially common in the section between Kirirom National Park and Preah Sihanouk. On Road 4 between Angk Snuol and Preah Sihanouk. They are especially common in the section between Kirirom National Park and Preah Sihanouk. One small off-road of Road 4, in Ream National Park near Preah Sihanouk. One small off-road of Road 4, in Ream National Park near Preah Sihanouk. In Preah Monivong National Park. In Preah Monivong National Park.

There is another good way to recognize Road 4 between Angk Snuol and Preah Sihanouk: in most sections, it has a distinctive wide, red-brownish shoulder on both sides of the road. NOTE: Near Phnom Penh, the soil of these shoulders tends to have a lighter, pinkish or beige colour. In the hills and closer to Preah Sihanouk, the soil tends to have a darker colour.

Oil palm plantations can only be found on Road 4, as well as some of its rural offroads, just north of Preah Nob. NOTE: Oil palm plantations are much more common in Malaysia and Indonesia. Only use this clue to region-guess if you are certain that you are in Cambodia, and not to identify the country.

Preah Monivong National Park in the south of the country has a unique and recognizable landscape. It is situated on a highland plateau. The soil is white and very rocky. The vegetation consists of stunted, windswept bushes and low trees. The foliage has a distinct dark green tint that contrasts with the white rocks. Some parts of the park are more forested but will still have the same rocky soil.

Road 41, southwest of Phnom Penh, has a recognizable look and road angle: It is a wide road, with a grey and very gravelly road surface It is a wide road, with a grey and very gravelly road surface It runs in a general NNE direction It runs in a general NNE direction The landscape close to the road is flat and agricultural. However, you can often see hills in the distance. The landscape close to the road is flat and agricultural. However, you can often see hills in the distance. NOTE: There are other roads that can look similar. Therefore, the road angle is very important to identify this road.

In the sections of Road 6 west of Siem Reap, to Sisophon, and Road 5, south of Sisophon to Krong Battambang, you can find power lines with unique poles that are found nowhere else in Cambodia. The pole tops have three horizontal beams, with hanging insulators on only one side. The bottom of the poles have indents.
The powerline from the previous tip continues on the section of Road 5 west of Sisophon. However, here the pole tops have insulators on both sides. The rest of the pole is identical however.

The southern section of Road 76, south of Krong Saen Monourom, has recognizable coverage: overcast weather, dark asphalt, the presence of outer road lines, and relatively crisp lines for Cambodian standards. Furthermore, a large part of the eastern half of this road runs through hilly terrain with dense jungle.

Most of the northern section of Road 76, between Lumphat and Mayura Wild Park, is recognizable too: it is a wide, unpaved road, with brown soil, and a semi-open jungle forest all around you. Weather conditions start off as overcast on the southern end of the road, and quickly improve the further north you go, with almost completely clear skies on the northern end. NOTE: There are other, smaller roads that can look similar. However, this road is by far the longest that has this distinct look.
Bilingual signs with Chinese writing can commonly be found in Preah Sihanouk.

Around the town of Pech Sreada, in the far east of Cambodia, you can find rubber tree plantations that were covered during the dry season, leading to a distinct look. In addition, the soil is very orange, making it easy to distinguish this area from other regions in Cambodia with rubber tree plantations.

Angkor Wat is a massive temple complex built by the historical Khmer Empire. It is located just north of Siem Reap and has extensive trekker coverage. It can be recognized by its dark, weathered stone buildings. While this location is unlikely to show up in competitive maps, it is extremely common in GeoGuessr’s official Cambodia map.

metas.title: Maximum sign

metas.title: Québec traffic cones
metas.description: Québec has unique orange and white striped traffic cones.

metas.title: Quebec rectangle markers
metas.description: You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary.

metas.title: Québec poles
metas.description: Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.

metas.title: Quebec pole stickers

metas.title: Québec bollards
metas.description: Québec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

metas.title: Exposed rocks
metas.description: The Canadian Shield extends through the eastern part of Canada. Therefore, you will commonly see exposed rocks on street view in the highlighted area.

general_rules.text: Each province has its own unique licence plates, some recognizable from afar even when blurred. Multiple provinces do not require front plates, which can be useful when deciding between provinces. NOTE: Since 2019, front plates are no longer required in New Brunswick. However, you should still expect to see them in older coverage. As well, all commercial vehicles in Newfoundland and Labrador are required to use front plates, and so it is possible to see them on vans and pickup trucks. You can click on the image to enlarge it.

The Dempster Highway (road numbers 5 and 8) connects the Klondike Highway (road number 2) in Yukon with the remote town of Inuvik in the Northwest Territories. It is very recognizable: it is an unpaved road with Generation 2 coverage, dark brown soil, and a tundra landscape with short trees. It is mostly hilly and mountainous, but the section between Fort McPherson and Inuvik is flat. Closer to Inuvik, the weather gets cloudy.

The Trans-Labrador Highway (road numbers 500 and 510) is a recognizable road, covered by Generation 4, mostly during sunny weather conditions. Thin pine trees line the side of the road, and it has a remote, cold, and northern feel. On many parts of the road, the sun is low in the sky. In addition, when the car drives past the city of Happy Valley-Goose Bay, it is common to see snow on the ground.

Quebec.text: Stop signs with the word ‘Arret’ are unique to Quebec in Canada.
Double sign posts on warning sings in Canada is unique to Quebec.
Quebec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.
Québec has unique bollards that are always attached to guardrails. They are long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

You will often find these yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts in Québec. In Québec City these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small. NOTE: Sometimes the markers will have different colours. Beware that Edmundston, in New Brunswick, uses these too.
Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.
Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.

The region around Rouyn-Noranda in northwestern Québec can mainly be characterised by the north-south grid, along with the slightly hilly landscape featuring many agricultural fields nestled between the forests, which have many shorter trees as well as thin birches.

The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is the most densely populated part of Canada. It is mostly flat and green, with a patchwork of agriculture and occasional forest cover. NOTE: This area can look similar to the Great Lakes region in the US.

Newfoundland.text: Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.
Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.
In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.
Newfoundland T-Intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.
Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.

The Balsam Fir is a very common species of tree found in Newfoundland. It has a Christmas tree-like appearance. NOTE: While most commonly found in Newfoundland, the Balsam Fir can also grow in other parts of Eastern Canada and the US. For an overview, see this map.

Ontario.text: Ontario speed limit signs may feature a black section at the bottom, with the words "km/h" or "begins" written in white.
Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones.
Ontario KM markers have a white square at the bottom, which is unique to the province.
You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.
In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.

Each province has its own unique kilometre markers that vary slightly. Notably, Ontario KM markers have a white square at the bottom, which is unique to the province. You can click on the image to enlarge it.

Some provinces have unique speed signs. Ontario speed limit signs may have a black section on the bottom with the words ‘km/h’ or ‘begins’ written in white. British Columbian signs also include the ‘km/h’ but lack the black section. Québec can sometimes have French on their speed limit signs. You can click on the image to enlarge it.
You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.
In Ontario, you will often see these types of guardrails. They consist of cylindrical wooden posts, held together by precisely three metal wires. Some posts are marked by a reflective white band.
Ontario uses distinct orange and black striped traffic cones. Québec, on the other hand, has unique orange and white striped traffic cones.

Alberta.text: Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.

Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently. NOTE: Some Alberta bollards have a yellow band between the two black bands, instead of a white one. Blue bands can also rarely be seen, particularly in and around Calgary, while green bands are rarely seen in and around Edmonton.
This guardrail, with small poles connected by three or four metal wires, can rarely be found on major highways in Alberta.

Manitoba.text: Manitoba license plates has green on both sides. Front plates are required.
You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.
You can sometimes find a green and white striped sticker on signposts in Manitoba.

Rural roads in Manitoba are organised in a grid and referred to only by their number and cardinal direction. Roads ending in N run east to west. Their numbers increase by one for every mile north of the US border. Roads ending in N run east to west. Their numbers increase by one for every mile north of the US border. Roads with E or W run north to south. They tell you their position relative to the principal meridian, located just west of Winnipeg. Roads with E or W run north to south. They tell you their position relative to the principal meridian, located just west of Winnipeg. For instance, this image was taken 105 miles north of the US border and 147 miles west of the principal meridian.

British Columbia.text: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.
The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.

These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.

British Columbia has black-and-white bollards with a thin, slightly curved shape. It is most commonly found on Vancouver Island, but can be found all throughout the province. NOTE: They can look superficially similar to the Alberta bollard. However, the thin shape and the wider spacing of the two black bands should help you tell them apart.
The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.

These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other. NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.
Signs in British Columbia are sometimes hung down from these unique signposts.
British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.
Western Canada is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta, and parts of Yukon. Outside these provinces, large mountains are rare to non-existent in Canada.

The landscape in the interior of southern British Columbia, mostly centred around the towns of Kamloops and Kelowna, has a distinct look. It is generally hilly and a little more arid than the rest of BC, The vegetation consists of sprawling brown grasslands, and pine tree forests on the hillsides.

New Brunswick.text:
You will often find these yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts in Québec.

In Québec City these markers will usually have a blue rectangle and markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small. NOTE: Sometimes the markers will have different colours. Beware that Edmundston, in New Brunswick, uses these too.

Stop signs with both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are most commonly found in New Brunswick.

NOTE: Such stop signs can rarely be found in other provinces.

Bins made of wood planks can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. These are most commonly octagonal, however they can have other shapes.

NOTE: Although they are most common in Newfoundland, they can also sometimes be seen in other provinces, such as New Brunswick.

Alberta license plates has red text on white background, it shows up as a red tint in the blur. It can be hard to see and it takes some time to get used to spotting it. Front plates are NOT required. Note: New Brunswick has similar license plates.
Stop signs in New Brunswick always have the word "Stop" written in France (Arrêt) in addition to the English word.

Stop signs in Québec always have the word "Stop" written in France (Arrêt).
Beware that "Arrêt" is also written on New Brunswick stop signs!

French is the majority language in Québec and parts of New Brunswick. NOTE: At the federal level, French has official status alongside English, so you can sometimes find bilingual signs in other parts of Canada. In addition, French is also spoken in several communities in Nova Scotia, Ontario and Manitoba.
You can find these rectangular markers on the sides of the roads in Québec. The colours can vary. NOTE: These can be rarely found on urban divided highways in New Brunswick.
These flat, yellow bollards can be found on the Trans-Canada highway in New Brunswick.
Stop signs with both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are most commonly found in New Brunswick. NOTE: Such stop signs can rarely be found in other provinces.
Like the stop signs, street signs in New Brunswick are also bilingual. Though unlike the stop signs, bilingual street signs are found in other French minority areas of Canada.
New Brunswick and Nova Scotia commonly use lampheads with a rectangular shape.

Saskatchewan.text: Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these white triangles. The number can vary.
Those white triangles(can be different ammount of them) on signposts of stop signs are unique to  Saskatchewan.

Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one.

Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Those white dashes between yellow lines are most commonly found in Saskatchewan. You can also sometimes find them in BC but the landscape will be way different.
Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.

Saskatchewan license plates has green text on white background, it shows up as a green tint in the blur. It can be hard to see and it takes some time to get used to spotting it. Front plates are NOT required.

Manitoba uses black and grey painted bollards. Most of the time an orange stripe will be present below the grey one. Wooden, rectangular bollards of this form are typically found further north in Manitoba. NOTE: Bollards in this format with just a black top are seen in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.
Signposts in Saskatchewan can feature these white triangles. The number can vary.
You can sometimes find white dashes between the yellow centre lines in Saskatchewan.

Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys, which means that the province can have a barren hilly landscape; much more so than the rest of the Canadian Great Plains, which tends to be really flat. NOTE: Some of this hilliness extends into southern Alberta and Manitoba.

Aspen trees are common in the forested parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They are recognizable by their white, birch-like trunks. In most seasons, they have regular green leaves, but in fall coverage, they turn a characteristic bright yellow colour.

Prince Edward Island.text:
Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint to it. Potato farming is also very common on PEI.

NOTE: This type of soil can occasionally be seen in certain areas of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.
Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.
Poles on Prince Edward Island usually feature a small white sticker.
Road signs in British Columbia can have green backsides. NOTE: Green backsides are also somewhat common on Prince Edward Island.

Within Eastern Canada, double yellow lines are most common in Nova Scotia, followed by Québec and Prince Edward Island. Ontario prefers single yellow lines for this purpose, but will occasionally use them. For some empirical research, please see this document.
Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint to it. Potato farming is also very common on PEI. NOTE: This type of soil can occasionally be seen in certain areas of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

Northwest Territories.text: The Northwest Territories has a black and white bollard with a cylindrical shape and two thick, black bands. NOTE: It looks very similar to the Alberta bollard. However, the Alberta bollard has thinner black bands.

Labrador.text: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden posts on guardrails have this pyramid shaped top. Occasionally, you can spot them on standalone posts and signposts as well.
You can spot these wooden boxes holding up signs in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Nova Scotia.text: Lamp arms on utility poles in Nova Scotia are usually curved and much shorter than in the rest of Canada. NOTE: Short lamp arms may occasionally be found in other parts of Canada.

Yukon.text: Yukon has a very northern, boreal landscape that is mostly hilly, sometimes with large mountains in the distance. Coniferous trees line the roads and the further north you go, the thinner and shorter the trees get. While this region recently got a lot of new Generation 4, older Generation 2 coverage is still very common.

spotlight.text: The Top of the World Highway west of Dawson City in Yukon has overcast Generation 2 coverage and is located mostly high up in the mountains, making it recognizable.
A group of motorcyclists can be seen in front of the Google car on this stretch of Highway 1 near Beaver Creek in Yukon.
The area near Drumheller, Alberta has distinct canyon-like treeless rock formations that comprise the landscape.
QC-167 and QC-113 are covered in Gen 3 and identifiable for their overcast autumn coverage, often with snow on the ground. In addition, a smudge can be seen on this road.
The Cape Breton Highlands in northeastern Nova Scotia have an unusual amount of elevation for Eastern Canadian standards. It is very forested, with a mix of broad-leaf trees and pine trees.

Route 430 on Newfoundland runs in a roughly south-southwest to north-northeast direction, with the road lines slightly washed out. It is located in a remote and sparsely populated part of the island. On many sections of the road, the coast is visible to your west. To your east, you will usually see low balsam fir forests, and occasionally an imposing wall of mountains in the far distance.

CL.name: Chile
CL.key_meta: Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides.

metas.title: Pole
metas.description: Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

metas.title: Empty slot under sign

from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: All yellow lines
metas.description: Within the Americas, all-yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile. These lines are typically seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall, as Chile usually uses all-white lines.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: Infrastructure - Green Dome Lamps
metas.description: Lamps that look like green domes can be seen in Copiapo.

metas.title: Trekker - Horse Trekker
metas.description: This horse trekker can be seen to the northwest of San Filipe.
metas.comparison: NOTE: A similar trekker can be found on the other side of the border in Argentina.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - B-710
metas.description: More Generation 4 Sunset coverage can be seen on B-710 and Ruta 5.
metas.comparison: On the B-710, a slight ridge can be seen to the west, while Ruta 5 is more open. Make sure to use the road angle or other clues before guessing.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Round Pole & Black Paint
metas.description: Round poles with black paint can be seen in the town of El Salvador.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Concepcion Lamps
metas.description: Blue rectangular lamps with a yellow stripe can be found in Concepción.

metas.title: Trekker - ALMA-OSF
metas.description: ALMA OSF can be recognized by the large radio telescopes and rural facilities.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Talca Lamps
metas.description: Grey lamps with a thin, flat top and a rounded underside can be found in Talca.

metas.title: Trekker - ACA
metas.description: ACA can be recognized by the many radio telescopes in a barren, snowy environment.

metas.title: Vegetation - Purple Flowers
metas.description: These purple flowers, named Large-leaved Lupines, can commonly be found along Ruta 240.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Orange Street Signs
metas.description: Orange street signs can be seen in the city of Lanco, present at almost every intersection.

metas.title: Landscape - Chiloé Landscape
metas.description: A rolling, agricultural landscape, comparable to New Zealand, can be seen on Isla Grande de Chiloé.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Similar looking landscapes exist in some other parts of the country, but usually more level.

metas.title: Car Meta - Toyota Hilux
metas.description: A grey Toyota Hilux, with various gear loaded and a snorkel on the front right, can be seen from around Baños Morales.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Letter Roads
metas.description: Chile uses a memorable regional road naming system, where the first letter increases between A and Y from north to south.

metas.title: Landscape - Eucalyptus
metas.description: Eucalyptus plantations combined with a somewhat dry climate are a good indicator that you are in southwestern Valparaíso.

metas.title: Car Meta - Conguillo National Park
metas.description: Conguillio National Park can be recognized by this white truck with visible side mirrors and an antenna on the front right.

metas.title: Landscape - A-31
metas.description: The A-31 can be recognised by its high altitude, with a steep drop into a valley to the north. The road also has Gen 3 sunset coverage.

metas.title: Landscape - Los Flamencos National Reserve
metas.description: Smooth mountains with a reddish tint are seen in Los Flamencos National Reserve. Salt pans are also a common sight. The reserve uses triple yellow lines.

metas.title: Trekker - Torres Del Paine
metas.description: The Torres del Paine area can be recognized by the sharp peaked mountains, and the trekker walking on a glacier along with other people in orange helmets.

metas.title: Vegetation - Chilean Rhubarb
metas.description: Chilean rhubarb can commonly be found on Isla Grande, and on the mainland east of it. Chilean rhubarb can be recognized by its large, cabbage-like appearance.

metas.title: Landscape - Puyehue National Park
metas.description: Puyehue National Park can be recognized by the dense vegetation surrounding the road. The pavement itself has triple yellow lines, and tar snakes are frequently seen.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Autumn Coverage
metas.description: Southern Aysén can be recognised by autumn coverage, having orange and red coloured vegetation. Keep in mind that not all coverage in this region will have fall colours.

metas.title: Landscape - Villa O'Higgins
metas.description: O’Higgins can be recognized by the large mountains to the east, often casting a shadow over the town. To the west, snow-capped mountains are seen further in the distance.

metas.title: Landscape - Alto Loa National Reserve
metas.description: Alto Loa National Reserve can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to snow-capped volcanoes. The reserve does not have any paved roads.

metas.title: Landscape - Nevado Tres Cruces National Park
metas.description: In the west, Nevado Tres Cruces National Park can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to a line of mountains. The sand has a reddish tint.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Ruta 9
metas.description: All yellow lines on a concrete road are a good indicator that you are on the paved section of Ruta 9, in the very south of Chile. The landscape tends to be barren, grassy, and treeless.

metas.title: Landscape - Nevado Tres Cruces National Park - Snow
metas.description: In the east of this park, the Google Car drives up a mountain pass with views of lightly snow-capped volcanoes and snow on the side of the road. The roads in the National Park are paved.

metas.title: Landscape - Pampa del Tamarugal
metas.description: The northern section of Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve can be recognized by the Tamarugo trees lining the road. The road itself is mediocre quality, and in a consistent north-west direction.

metas.title: Landscape - Pan de Azucar National Park
metas.description: Pan de Azucar National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, little vegetation, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage

metas.title: Landscape - Llanos de Challe National Park
metas.description: Llanos de Challe National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, juniper plants, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage.

metas.title: Landscape - Ruta 41 - White Lines
metas.description: Part of Ruta 41 is located in a valley, with snowy mountains seen in the distance. Many trees and vineyards can commonly be seen toward the west. Triple white lines west of the middle between Balala and Miraflores.

metas.title: Landscape - Ruta 1
metas.description: Ruta 1 is a coastal road that is easily recognized by the wall of mountains to the east, and the Pacific Ocean to the west. This image shows the various weather conditions faced on the road to help you make closer guesses.

metas.title: Landscape - A11 - Barren
metas.description: After crossing the Lluta River at Poconchile, the Ruta 11 continues out of the valley and up into the mountains. The road is all newly paved (except for a few small segments with ongoing construction) and is generally quite wide. This section of Ruta 11 features:
metas.comparison: The landscape is bare of vegetation until around Zapahuira, east of which the landscape becomes open and covered with small green bushes.

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description: Chilean bollards are similar to Spanish style bollards, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are not super common. While regular bollards are somewhat rare in Chile, you may sometimes find this orange, temporary bollard, with two white stripes at the top.

metas.title: Landscape - Lauca National Park
metas.description: East of Putre, Ruta 11 enters Lauca National Park which has a flatter landscape, with tall snow-capped mountains in the background, and features unique Andean Plateau vegetation like Peruvian feather grass and the recognizable cushion plant yareta (Azorella compacta). You can also find Chilean bollards lining the road, which are extremely rare.
metas.comparison: Lauca can look very similar to other areas in the east Andes of northern Chile, but it’s recognizable for the iconic Volcán Parinacota, a tall snow-capped volcano that stands alone and away from other mountain ridges. It’s visible from basically every location in the park, though it can be shrouded by clouds.

general_rules.text: Chilean phone codes will sometimes have a two digit area code in front, followed by seven digits. The patterns of the codes are easily memorable. Most of the central states also have different area codes for specific provinces, which can help you make accurate guesses.

Antofagasta.text: A rockier, and more uneven ridge can be seen in Antofagasta.

Orange lamps can most often be seen in Calama and Chañaral, and rarely in Antofagasta.

NOTE: Orange lamps can rarely be found in other smaller cities. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

Atacama.text:
This brownish red soil can sometimes be seen in Atacama province.

NOTE: This is most reliable in Generation 3. This soil can be seen in other provinces in Generation 4.
San Pedro de Atacama can be recognized by its clay brick walls, commonly with triangles at the top.
Poles in Arica feature white paint with a black number, while the other cities in the Atacama Desert feature poles with yellow paint. Keep in mind the paint may have faded, making it look white.

The Atacama is an extremely arid desert covering the northern third of Chile. Some parts of it experience the lowest rainfall on the planet. As a result, many locations in this desert are almost completely devoid of any vegetation: you will often just see sand and bare rock without any plants in sight anywhere.

NOTE: The Atacama Desert also covers parts of southern Peru, western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina.

Along the Lluta River, the Ruta 11 passes through a wide valley lined by sloping, sandy mountains that often feature distinctly round rock protrusions.
The valley is home to a large amount of agriculture relative to other parts of the Atacama Desert. You’ll often see sizable green fields lined by bushes, trees, or wooden fences, as well as bunches of planted Mexican fan palms.
A railroad track also follows the Lluta River on both sides, so if you’re in a green valley next to both a river and a railroad, you’re almost certainly on Ruta 11.

The Atacama is an extremely arid desert covering the northern third of Chile. Some parts of it experience the lowest rainfall on the planet. As a result, many locations in this desert are almost completely devoid of any vegetation: you will often just see sand and bare rock without any plants in sight anywhere. NOTE: The Atacama Desert also covers parts of southern Peru, western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina.
These rocky, uneven mountains are most commonly seen in Atacama and northern Coquimbo.
This brownish red soil can sometimes be seen in Atacama region. NOTE: This is most reliable in Generation 3. This soil can be seen in other regions in Generation 4.

Arica.text: A slight, sandy ridge with a gradual incline can be seen in Arica.

The province of Arica y Parinacota can be recognized by the smooth, sandy mountains that may look slightly eroded, or have bulbous formations. Valleys are also common, which are rarely seen in other parts of Chile.

The region of Arica y Parinacota can be recognized by the smooth, sandy mountains that may look slightly eroded, or have bulbous formations. Valleys are also common, which are rarely seen in other parts of Chile.

Puerto Montt.text: This lamp, with a silver top and grey bottom, can be found in Puerto Montt and Temuco.

Coquimbo.text: These rocky, uneven mountains are most commonly seen in Atacama and northern Coquimbo.

Eulychnia acida, commonly known as cactus ácido or copao, is a cactus species endemic to Chile, where it is primarily distributed in the semi-arid regions of the country. Its range includes: Atacama Region, Coquimbo Region,and Valparaíso Region.

Araucania.text:
Monkey puzzles, scientifically named Araucaria araucana, are found in far eastern Araucania.

NOTE: Monkey puzzles can also be found on the other side of the Argentinian border.
Narrow roads with trees on both sides can commonly be seen in the provinces of Bio Bio and Araucania.
Narrow roads with trees on both sides can commonly be seen in the regions of Bio Bio and Araucania.
Monkey puzzles, scientifically named Araucaria araucana, are found in far eastern Araucania. NOTE: Monkey puzzles can also be found on the other side of the Argentinian border.

Santiago.text: The region around Santiago can be recognized by its semi-arid climate, having dry hills and scattered vegetation.
The Google car can be seen towing a white and silver trailer with the word ‘Outback’ north of the Chilean National Zoo in Santiago.
Compared to the area around Santiago, the Maule province has a similar look. However, it has a Mediterranean climate, and is generally greener.
The region around Santiago can be recognized by its semi-arid climate, having dry hills and scattered vegetation.

Los Lagos.text: Lush green valleys, with rocky mountains and often overcast coverage, can be seen in southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén.
Lush green valleys, with rocky mountains and often overcast coverage, can be seen in southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén.

Valparaiso.text: Lamps in Santiago very commonly have photocells. You will rarely find them in other cities such as Valparaiso, Osorno and Loncoche.

Bio Bio.text: Ruta 181 leading up to Alto Bio Bio National Reserve has triple yellow lines, looks similar to the reserve but with more vegetation.
A vast, mostly treeless landscape combined with triple yellow lines are seen in Alto Bio Bio National Reserve. While the reserve may look dry, there is a distinct cold and high altitude feel.

Punta Arenas.text:
Puerto Williams, the southernmost town covered by street view, can be recognized by this white pickup truck with visible side mirrors.

NOTE: The Puerto Williams coverage is located fairly far away from the normal car coverage in Chile. The nearest normal car coverage is in Fuerte Bulnes, near Punta Arenas.

O'Higgins.text: It is endemic to a small area of central Chile between southern Coquimbo, Valparaíso, Santiago, O'Higgins, and northern Maule regions. They are highly concentrated around Viña del Mar.

Concepcion.text: Concepcion pines, scientifically named Pinus radiata, can be recognized by their puffy needles. They are most commonly found in Bio Bio, where the city of Concepcion is located, and less commonly in Ñuble and Araucania.

Concepcion pines, scientifically named Pinus radiata, can be recognized by their puffy needles. They are most commonly found in Bio Bio, where the city of Concepcion is located, and less commonly in Ñuble and Araucania.

Maule.text: Compared to the area around Santiago, the Maule region has a similar look. However, it has a Mediterranean climate, and is generally greener. Vineyards are also commonly seen in this region.

CN.name: China
CN.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (4 regions covered).

Coverage.text: Coverage in mainland China is limited to several small spots, mainly in or near major urban areas on the east coast. A significant portion of the coverage is considered hidden, which is also shown on this map. Hidden means it won’t show up on Google Maps, however you can still access it in the Map Making App.

Museums.text: A significant portion of the coverage was taken inside museums and can be found in many cities, however a majority of the covered museums are located in and around Beijing and Shanghai.

Ancienttowns.text: Ancient cities with coverage can be found along the east coast in Zhoucun, northeast of Xuzhou, in Yangzhou, west of Jiaxing and west of Zhangzhou.

Urban.text: Coverage taken outside in modern urban areas can be found in Beijing, Yangzhou, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chengdu.

spotlight.text: This section contains more in-depth descriptions of all coverage considered pinpointable in mainland China. For a complete guide to the Chinese coverage, read this document.
The Palace Museum (commonly referred to as the Forbidden City) is a massive palace in the centre of Beijing.
By the Today Art Museum in Beijing you can find this modern urban street with several cafes and bars along the road. In front of the museum you can also find this uncanny statue.
The parking area outside Sichuan Museum in Chengdu has a lot of greenery.
The Hubei Museum in Wuhan can be recognised by its palace-like architecture with grey roofs.
The Museum of silk production in Hangzhou can be recognised by the rounded glass facade and the fountain by the front.
Shanghai Long Museum can be recognised by the boxy concrete main building.
Suzhou Museum can be recognised by the white and grey symmetric angular architecture.
The Yangzhou Museum can be recognised by the beige rounded stone building.
The ancient city of Zhoucun is the only pinpointable ancient city in China, and can be recognised by the street going straight north to south.

CX.name: Christmas Island
CX.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (3 regions covered).

Christmas.text: The built-up areas are in the northeast. The rest of the island is mostly covered by dense forest.

Boat.text: There is a boat trekker near the north coast of the island. Some of the boat’s white-coloured deck pokes through the blur. Much of the trekker closely hugs the coast; here you can see the steep, rocky coastline of Christmas Island.

Trail.text: There is an abundance of smaller trail trekkers all over the island. These are mostly surrounded by very dense foliage, but occasionally you can encounter interesting sights like beaches and lookouts. NOTE: Click here for a larger map of their locations.

spotlight.text: An exception to the road coverage mostly having car meta is the coastal Jln Pantai road, where a regular trekker was used. On this road, you will not see the back of the car, just a trekker blur.
The harbour area is recognizable by the large cranes that are visible from many vantage points.
This golf course trekker is on the northeast coast. In some places, the Google car also drove on this golf course.

Christmas Island is famous for its red crabs. Near Ethel Beach, you can find a trekker walking among hundreds of these crabs. Another smaller trekker where you can see crabs is near The Dales, on the West Coast. Throughout the island, you can find references on signs to these crabs. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

CC.name: Cocos Islands
CC.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (3 regions covered).

Island.text: This unique car with a snorkel at the front right and the edges of the bed visible is found on West Island.

Bantam.text: This white car with the rear edges visible is found in Bantam. NOTE: The car may be fully blurred. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.
Bantam Village can be recognized by the cross-hatched brick pavement.

Runway.text: The Cocos Islands runway can be recognized by it being the widest paved road on the island, with mowed grass on both sides of the runway and this follow car.

spotlight.text: Cocos Islands has many trekkers along the coast. Most of them will be walking on white sand, with the ocean to one side and palms the other.

Direction Island can be recognized by the beaches having significantly more litter compared to the other islands. Bricks, styrofoam and dead coral can be seen along some portions of the coast. In addition, the trekker can be seen walking between many palms inland.
The inland trekker on Pulau Luar (Horsburgh Island) can be recognized by the dry, yellow grass, and more sparse vegetation.
This medium boat with a large seating capacity can be seen from West Island to Bantam.
This small boat with black bars at the rear can be seen in the north.

This small dark grey boat with a woman sitting at the back can be seen in the south. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

CO.name: Colombia
CO.key_meta: Signposts in Colombia are made of white thin metal and have a distinct cross on the back.

metas.title: Colombian cross
metas.description: Signposts in Colombia are made of white thin metal and have a distinct cross on the back.
metas.comparison: In the photo, green checkmarks show the "real" Colombian cross, and red X's show the ones that aren't right.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: Yellow plates
