metas.description: In South America, yellow license plates are almost exclusive to Colombia. Commercial vehicles in Colombia may have white plates.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: Infrastructure - Tinto Bus
metas.description: This red bus drives in the town (not the country) Armenia.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Valle de Cauca Polepaint
metas.description: Yellow, with black numbers. Several digits can be in one row.

metas.title: Landscape - Deep grey & stony soil in Gen 3
metas.description: This type of soil can be found in towns near the pacific coast.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Rainy Coverage
metas.description: Rainy coverage is most common on the highways 20, 24, 50 and 64.

metas.title: Trekker - Trebal Resort Trekker
metas.description: This trekker can be recognized by the unique pavement and houses.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Foggy & Rainy Coverage
metas.description: If you see rainy coverage, combined with strong fog, you're on the 64.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Embalse Calima
metas.description: Large lake, mostly winter coverage. A small stretch also has summer coverage.

metas.title: Landscape - Unique Road - 78 west of Pailitas
metas.description: This road is characterised by low clouds and a towering mountain in the east.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Electricity Counter - Oval
metas.description: Usually pretty tall with oval windows, circle windows might not be as trustworthy.
metas.comparison: Very common as there are few plastic counters in this region.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Tumaco
metas.description: If you see many puddles and a pavement out of '+' shaped stones, you're in Tumaco.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - La Florida
metas.description: Rainy coverage with very orange-brown soil can be found on this road to La Florida.

metas.title: Car Meta - San Andres
metas.description: Coverage on the Caribbean island of San Andrés was taken by this distinct white car.

metas.title: Car Meta - Leticia
metas.description: This unique vehicle can be found in and around Leticia, the Southernmost town in Colombia.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The long concrete blocks seen in the bottom left corner are a reliable way of recognising the road North of Leticia.

metas.title: Landscape - Guatape Hill
metas.description: This striking cone-shaped mountain can often be seen from the surrounding area of Guatape.

metas.title: Landscape - Northern Landscape
metas.description: The Northern part of the country is characterised by white, sandy soil and an arid landscape.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Unique Road - Tame to Arauca
metas.description: On this road, you can see a sunset through the clouds. It's not always easy to recognize, however.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Double Google Car - Aguachica
metas.description: This instance of a second google car can be seen on Carrera 4, an offroad of the 45 near Aguachica.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - "Gen 5" Glitch
metas.description: A camera glitch that makes a part of the image look very saturated can be found in southern Colombia.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Sogamoso Lake
metas.description: If you see a lake, paired with an overexposed Gen 4 camera, you're probably on this lake south of Sogamoso.

metas.title: Vegetation - Wide Trees
metas.description: These wide trees, usually near fences, are found in Northern regions, especially near Monteria and Sincelejo.

metas.title: Car Meta - Providencia
metas.description: The island of Providencia, located roughly 90 kilometres North of San Andrés, is home to this unique grey truck.

metas.title: Agriculture - Aracataca Cut Palms
metas.description: These palms where the crown has been cut, are very often found near Aracataca and some smaller towns North of it.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Unique Road - Tame to Hato Corozal
metas.description: On this road, you can see a slight sunset through the clouds. It is pretty flat, with mountains in the Northwest.

metas.title: Misc - Afro-Colombians
metas.description: As a result of slave trade, the Pacific coast of Colombia is home to an overwhelming majority of Afro-Colombians.

metas.title: Vegetation - Kapok Tree
metas.description: The Kapok tree can be found throughout Colombia, but is most common between the central and eastern mountain range.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Buenaventura Truck Spam Road
metas.description: The stretch of the 40 to Buenaventura is an important route for trucks, so if you see many trucks, it's worth a thought.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Villavicencio Bike Lane Road
metas.description: If you see a bike lane, and get East of Andes vibes, you're most likely on the road through Los Tobitos to Villavicencio.

metas.title: Landscape - Swamp Roads
metas.description: The 74, the 78 and a few other roads more north have very swampy parts, you can see on the map where these are by zooming.

metas.title: Infrastructure - TransLago vans
metas.description: TransLogo vans are common throughtout Boyaca Department. You will most often see them on the routes Tunja-Sogamoso and Tunja-Duitama.

metas.title: Coverage Meta - Double Google Car - Villavicencio
metas.description: This instance of a second google car can be seen on the east-west road, directly south of Guayuriba River, which is south of Villavicencio.

metas.title: Agriculture - Common Guava
metas.description: Common Guava mostly appears in the valley between the western and the central mountain range in Colombia, but it can also appear in other valleys.

metas.title: Landscape - East of Andes Landscape
metas.description: East of the Andes lies a vast lowland called Llanos. It is characterised by open tropical grasslands, savannas with scattered trees, small areas of forest and seasonal flooding.
metas.comparison: Since it's to the east of the Andes, you may see mountains in the west, but never in the east.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Sarawak Pole
metas.description: Asymmetrical poles with a "Sarawak" extension (a vertical stalk coming out the top), can often be found East of Andes. Note that this pole is not 100%, and has been spotted elsewhere.

Antioquia.text: These pole markings with one short black strip on the top and bottom, and a longer yellow section in the middle, are most commonly found in the Antioquia department. Sometimes, you can find them in the Cordoba department as well.

Large amounts of banana plants in plantations are commonly found in different areas.

Paired with Cloudy Gen 3 Coverage, they're most common in Northwestern Antioquia.
In general, banana plantation can be found mostly in Quindio and Magdalena, sometimes in Northwest-Antioquia and Cordoba, and rarely in surrounding provinces of Quindio.

These pole markings with one short black strip on the top and bottom, and a longer yellow section in the middle, are most commonly found in the Antioquia department. Sometimes, you can find them in the Cordoba department as well.

Barranquilla.text: White Transmetro buses can be found in Barranquilla.
In Barranquilla, you can often find this bollard with roadnames on intersections.
Houses with roofs like this are commonly found along the coast, especially near Cartagena and Barranquilla.
The uniquely shaped supporting metal piece can be found in Barranquilla. (Similar to the Providencia design)
Providencia street lights are green and supported by a trapezoidal sheet of metal underneath. (The metal sheet without a green lamp can also be found in Barranquilla)

You can recognise the narrow Ruta 90 landbridge between Barranquilla and Cienaga thanks to the dashed yellow lines and shallow bodies of water next to the road. Open ocean can often be seen to the north.

NOTE: In the older Generation 3 coverage, you will also see tall mountains in the distance.

Bogota.text: H-shaped lamp attachment plates can be found in Bogota.

Paramos refers to alpine tundra ecosystems located in the mountains. These kinds of regions are easy to guess by how little vegetation grows here. The best clue is these odd looking pants. ( giant rosette plants ).

Note by MB: In my experience, this appears most commonly south of Bogota, still in the capital district.

Cauca.text: Sugarcane will mainly be found in Cauca and Valle de Cauca.
A Second Google Car is visible in many random spots. The most prominent spots are the 26 in Cauca, Vda. Chontaduro (near Popoyan) and the road between Pital and Tarqui.
Sugar cane is grown along the Cauca river in Valle del Cauca and neighbouring departments.

Vichada.text: Vichada is characterize by hazy Gen 4 coverage and Red Dirt.
Santa Rosalia is the only town covered in Vichada. So if you see red/orange dirt in an urban Gen 4 loc, you should go there.

Quindio.text: In Quindio you will commonly find banana plantations behind hedges.
This palm is found in mountainous regions of Colombia, mainly in Quindio, as the name suggests.
In the states surrounding Quindio you will find smaller banana plantations along the road not behind hedges.

Valle del Cauca.text: If you see these poletops you will find yourself in Valle Del Cauca.

Putumayo.text: This constellation can be found on the 65 in Caqueta and the 45 in Putumayo.

Santander.text: This unique cobblestone pavement is found is the historic town of Barichara, Santander.

Medellin.text: This tree is found mainly around Medellin, but it has been spotted in other random spots.
Rectangular lamp attachment plates can be found mainly in Medellin, sometimes further North, especially in Monteria and Cucuta.

The coffee belt stretches in the valley between Medellin and Cali. In the North, you will only find it near the Venezuelan border.

Olives and Tea have a very similar distribution.

Sucre.text: If you see a swamp road with extremely sunny coverage, you're probably on the 74 in Sucre.

Pereira.text: Green or yellow, modern bus. Often on a dedicated bus lane. Found in Pereira metropolitan area.

Huila.text: Cacti are most commonly found in the North near Valledupar. Sometimes they can appear in Huila, too.

Risaralda.text: Yellow paint with red numbers. Found all over Risaralda and the towns of Istmina and Quibdo in Choco.
Guadua Bamboo plantations are found mainly in Caldas, but also in the adjecent Tolima, Quindio and Risaralda.

Magdalena.text: In Magdalena you will often see banana plantations in a dry sandy/dirty area with mountains to your east.

Cundinamarca.text: This stick on the camera can be found between El Guio and El Boral (near the Cundinamarca-Meta border near Villavicencio)
This spanish bollard is mostly found in Cundinamarca, the area surrounding Bogotá, but also on the 40 towards Villavicencio.
This european-style (specifically spanish style bollard) is found in Cundinamarca, but also on the 40 towards Villavicencio.

La Guajira.text: This landscape is typical of the far Northern province of La Guajira: extreme dryness, low vegetation and occasional cacti.

You can often recognise the Uribia-Puerto Bolivar road because of La Guajira landscape (extreme dryness, low vegetation and occasional cacti), the straightness and the train track always present to the East.

Cali.text: Gen 4 with the white car has no coverage south of Cali, very little around Medellín, and forms a curved pattern around Medellín.

Guaviare.text: The only road in Guaviare goes from to Guaviare (city), and continues south up until Vda. El Trueno. It can be recognized by the orange-looking dust on the road.

Casanare.text: Oilpalms can be found mainly in Meta and Casanare. They are also very common around the 45 near Fundacion and Aracataca. Sometimes, you can find them in Barrancabermeja.

Bucaramanga.text: Gen 3 with the white-blue car follows a straight line between Cartagena and Medellín, has partial coverage along Route 80 west of Bosconia, as well as along Route 45 north of Bucaramanga and east of Medellín.

Gen 4 coverage with the grey car is not found north of Montería, has a gap between Bucaramanga and Bogotá, forms a 'staircase' pattern with right angles at Medellín and Bogotá, covers areas around Bucaramanga, and has a missing section around Popayán.

Arauca.text: On the road in Arauca and in the city of Arauca in northeastern Colombia, there is virtually only cloudy, bad weather coverage. Furthermore, there was a small camera glitch where you can see this small rift northeast of the driving direction.

Cordoba.text: In Colombia you will most commonly find these trees that appear to have a knot on top of their trunk in the dark red areas. The province of Cordoba has the most gen 4 out of the others so if you see these in gen 4 consider Cordoba. (If the area is flat/semi hilly, You can find these trees in the mountains aswell everywhere)

Meta.text:
In southern Colombia, around the city of Pasto, there are hilly fields that are unique in that they are bordered by hedges. The hedges are very thick and form very distinctive lines on the hills. It almost gives off a “British” vibe.
If you are sure that it is Colombia, this is a very good meta, but such fields with hedges also occur in Ecuador.

!!
In very rare cases, such hedges on hills can also occur in other parts of Colombia.
!!

spotlight.text: This landscape is typical of the far Northern province of La Guajira: extreme dryness, low vegetation and occasional cacti. In addition, you can often recognise the Uribia-Puerto Bolivar road because of this landscape, the straightness and the train track always present to the East.

You can recognise the narrow Ruta 90 landbridge between Barranquilla and Cienaga thanks to the dashed yellow lines and shallow bodies of water next to the road. Open ocean can often be seen to the north. NOTE: In the older Generation 3 coverage, you will also see tall mountains in the distance.

Intersections in the coastal city of Barranquilla are commonly marked by small concrete poles (mojones) bearing street names. For example, this image was taken at the intersection of Carrera 42 and Calle 68.
Coverage on the Caribbean island of San Andrés was taken by this distinct white car.
Providencia street lights are green and supported by a trapezoidal sheet of metal underneath. NOTE: The uniquely shaped supporting metal piece can also be found in Barranquilla.

CR.name: Costa Rica
CR.key_meta: Area codes are moderately useful to learn for Costa Rica.

metas.title: Alto
metas.description: Costa Rica, Guatemala, Panama and Mexico are the only countries using the word "Alto" on their stop signs.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta World - Stop Signs

general_rules.text: Area codes are moderately useful to learn for Costa Rica.

Poles are sometimes marked with large black or white stickers, containing multiple lines of text. The first digit of the topmost number is province-specific. For more specific information, please see this research document created by L’Heureux Traité.

Asymmetrical pole tops with one insulator on one side of the pole and two on the other are found in and around San José. NOTE: Fully asymmetrical pole tops with all insulators on one side of the pole can be found all across the country.

The majority of oil palm plantations are found along the coast in Puntarenas province. A few smaller plantations are located in Limón province. NOTE: A few oil palms can be found here and there throughout the country, especially on the east coast but they’re not part of any plantations.

Sugarcane plantations can be found in multiple areas across the country, but the major areas are usually distinguishable based on landscape. In the southern area around San Isidro de El General and Buenos Aires you can find sugarcane plantations in bloom with silvery tufts of strands at the top of the plants.

1Mcfzfq.text: White pole plates with black lettering are specific to the Greater Metropolitan Area. They are usually attached to the pole using metal bands, although these may sometimes be missing.

1Aooncd.text: Usually blue lettering forming a P-XXXXX code with or without the accompanying white background can be found in western Cartago province.

Teak2.text: Teak is recognisable for their tall straight trunks and round glossy, yellow-green leaves and is most common in Guanacaste.

Iio7Tjd.text: Guanacaste trees can be recognised by their thick trunk and characteristically large, umbrella-shaped crown. They are mostly seen in the eponymous Guanacaste province.

spotlight.text: The only concrete highways are the eastern stretch of Ruta Nacional 18, and the divided Pan-American Highway (RN 1) from Liberia to the intersection with RN 18.

Wind turbines are found in a few clusters, mainly in Guanacaste province, but also southwest of Cartago, over the province border in San José province. In Guanacaste, you’ll find them around La Fortuna, south and northwest of Tilarán, around Santa Cruz, and quite far north of Liberia around road 917.
Bright white soil roads likely place you just north of the city of Liberia, Guanacaste province.

HR.name: Croatia
HR.key_meta: Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and a red or white reflector.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and a red or white reflector. From the top, they are shaped like a triangle. Hungarian bollards are similar, but the black part with the reflector is positioned further from the top.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and red or white reflector. From the top, it is shaped like a triangle.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The distance between the top end and the reflector is shorter than in Hungary.

metas.title: Belt + Straight Legs Croatia/Bosnia
metas.description: White Belt: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal, Germany, Hungary. > Non-Pointed Shoes: Croatia/Bosnia, Portugal. > Straight legs: Croatia/Bosnia.

general_rules.text: Croatian landlines typically start with a zero followed by the area code.

Hungary.text: The north-eastern region of Croatia is mostly flat and features a lot of agriculture. It is similar in terms of landscape to Hungary and north-western Serbia.

Zagreb.text: The region north and west of Zagreb is hilly and agricultural.

Adriatic.text: The Adriatic coast features rocky mountains similar to those seen in Montenegro or Albania. Shrubs are more common instead of trees along the coast, especially in the south. This coastal region has a lot of islands and peninsulas.

Houses and walls made of beige brick are common on the Adriatic coast. They often feature green shutters. NOTE: Similar architecture can also be found in some regions in Italy. Additionally, Croatian shutters can also be white, beige etc.

Istria.text: The north-western region of Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, sometimes has distinct red soil.

Indicator.text: Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and Italian are typically found in Istria, especially in the western cities.

spotlight.text: Croatia’s capital Zagreb has a distinct big city feel. Apartment blocks can be seen throughout the city. The northern part of the city is hilly. Furthermore, Zagreb has blue electric trams. NOTE: In addition to regular car coverage, Zagreb also has various urban sidewalk trekkers, often made with a Generation 2 camera.
Zagreb and Osijek are the only two cities in Croatia with trams.
The region northeast of Zadar is recognizable as it is flat with a mountain ridge visible in the distance north.

There are a lot of vineyards around the town of Ilok, near the Serbian border, west of Novi Sad. You can find vineyards in other parts of Croatia as well, but they are most common in this area. If you see lots of vineyards in a northeastern Croatian landscape, you are more often than not near Ilok.
Traffic lights in Rijeka are held up by long blue poles that extend out over the road. These are exclusive to the city.
The town of Petrinja was severely damaged by an earthquake in 2020. As a result, many buildings can be seen ruined and undergoing repair.
The city of Dubrovnik in the far south of coastal Croatia is famous for its beautifully preserved medieval city walls, which can be seen from many points in and around the Old Town.
These tall cypress trees are commonly found near the southern tip of Croatia.

CW.name: Curaçao
CW.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (1 regions covered).

metas.title: One Storey Bungalows
metas.description:
Much of the architecture on Curaçao consists of simple, one storey bungalows that are pastel coloured.
Metal roofs are common on smaller shacks, while tiled roofs can be seen on more expensive houses.
Additionally, multi storey villas can sometimes be seen.

Rural.text: The western half of Curaçao is characterised by a semi-arid rural landscape with green, but dry hills. Houses are spread apart, with the roads in the west quite narrow in width.

spotlight.text: A line of wind turbines can be seen at this wind farm toward the southeast of Curaçao. The coverage is also notably rainy.

The Queen Juliana Bridge is a wide four lane bridge in Willemstad. It can be recognized by the yellow and blue guardrails, and the view over the city. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

CY.name: Cyprus
CY.key_meta: Cyprus uses A, B, E, and F roads, and they are grouped by their first digit.

general_rules.text: Cyprus uses A, B, E, and F roads, and they are grouped by their first digit. NOTE: E and F roads are located near the B road with the matching first digit. This is useful because B roads are easier to find.
Each of the 5 provinces uses a two-digit area code, starting with a 2.
Cyprus uses four-digit postal codes, grouped by region. They can be found on street signs, and are denoted by either T.K. or T.T. The first digits can be useful to memorise.

Image%20(4).text: Being a small island, the terrain will be the easiest way to narrow down your location. Most of the country is hilly to mountainous, with the centre having the highest elevation, that you can use to orient yourself.

Cyprus%20White%20Rock.text: While the bright exposed limestone rock is a good clue for the country, it is mainly found along its southern coast.

E5Pzgxx.Jpeg(2).text: On the other hand, reddish soil is found in the interior and northwest of the country.

Cyprus%20Wine%20Regions.text: Vineyards are found more towards the southwest of Cyprus.

Cyprus%20Yellow%20Flowers.text: Wild Mustard, which looks like bushes of yellow flowers, while possible to find on most of Cyprus, is most common in these areas, mainly in the eastern half of the country.

Cyprus%20Paphos%20Forest.text: The Paphos Forest nature reserve consists of windy mountain roads with red soil on the sides, passing through the mostly uninhabited Mediterranean forest. You will not see any bollards in the reserve, with few exceptions.

Cyprus%20North%20Valley.text: In the northeast of Cyprus, you will often be able to see the Kyrenia Mountain ridge to the north, overlooking the otherwise flat farmland.

Cyprus%20Or%20Zacatecas.text: Dark red fields, even if covered in vegetation, are a good clue for northern Cyprus and Famagusta, the far eastern region.

Cyprus%20Famagusta.text: Famagusta can easily be recognised by the mostly flat landscape, with lots of red fields. Maybe more importantly though, all of the coverage is shitcam. NOTE: Shitcam is quite rare in the rest of Cyprus.

Cyprus%20Wind%20Torbines.text: Wind turbines are found in two main clusters on Cyprus: west of Larnaca in the east, and southwest of Anogyra, near the Limassol-Paphos subdivision border.

Cyprus%20Ne%20Torbines.text: The wind turbines in the east are built on sandy rolling hills, surrounded by agricultural fields .

Cyprus%20Sw%20Torbines.text: The wind turbines in the SW are located within the Oreites Forest, a shrubby hill surrounded by more extreme elevation. There is a noticeable incline towards the coast, which is often visible to the southwest.

Cyprus%20Or%20Slovenia%20Maybe%20Bonsia.text: A different kind of bollard with a black top, resembling those found in Slovenia for example, can sometimes be found in north-eastern Cyprus. NOTE: The presence of regular Cypriot bollards does not exclude the highlighted region.

spotlight.text: Snow coverage can be found on a few roads southeast of the Cyprus island label, near the Holy Monastery of Panagia Machaira.
Dashed blue lines between the outer and inner road markings can be seen on a few roads around Mount Olympus.
Banana plantations can be found along the western coast around Peyia.
With a Russian-speaking population of around 17%, many commercial signs in Limassol feature Russian translations.

CZ.name: Czechia
CZ.key_meta: Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants. The same design is also found in Slovakia.

metas.title: Arrow-shaped signs
metas.description: Czechia uses arrow-shaped directional signs with a filled in tip. Due to the shape, they are recognizable from behind.

metas.title: North - Timber Framed Houses
metas.description: Timber framed houses in Czechia are mostly found along the northern parts of the German border.

metas.title: Northwest - Single Pane Windows
metas.description: It is more common to see houses with single pane windows in the northwestern parts of the country.

metas.title: North - White Stripes
metas.description: Dark wooden houses, with white stripes shining through the wood, are common in most of northern Czechia.

metas.title: Pair Poles
metas.description: Czechia and Slovakia most commonly use wide, round concrete poles, which are quite often attached in pairs.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: North - Dark Wooden Supports
metas.description: Houses with thick, dark wooden poles supporting the upper floors are common in the northernmost parts of the country.

metas.title: Rolling Landscape
metas.description:
The Czech landscape is fairly rolling, with a lot of hills and altitude changes, but not a lot of tall mountains.
Generally speaking, Slovakia has more mountains, but also more completely flat areas.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: České Budějovice - Baroque Architecture
metas.description:
A variant of baroque architecture called Selské Baroko (folk baroque) can be found in the region surrounding České Budějovice.
The style is characterised by highly decorated walls, with the setting being small villages rather than towns and cities.

general_rules.text: The first digit of road numbers can be anything between 1-6. Though, roads starting with 6 are scattered across most of the country. There are three exceptions, being roads 7, 8 and 9, which all start in Prague and go to the north and northwest. Roads starting with 1-5 are mostly distributed as the map shows, with some overlap and exceptions mainly due to longer, two-digit roads.

Four-digit bike paths follow a geographical pattern, increasing clockwise, starting in Southern Bohemia. They do not show up on Google Maps, and as such remembering the general pattern is necessary to make them useful. Single- and two-digit bike paths are shown on this map, however they are far less useful to know. NOTE: Paths starting with A are unique to Prague, regardless how big the number. Some paths spill into neighbouring regions.

Czech phone numbers are typically made up of 9 digits, of which the first 1-3 digits are the area code. Note that if the first digit is 6 or higher, it does not indicate a specific area. They’re not very common. NOTE: Slovak phone numbers typically begin with a 0.

Moravia.text:
Town houses in Moravia typically have two distinctive features:

--- NOTE:

Town houses in Moravia typically have two distinctive features: Houses have the long side parallel to the road and are often connected in large groups. Houses have the long side parallel to the road and are often connected in large groups. Front doors are abnormally large, similar in size and shape to barn doors. Front doors are abnormally large, similar in size and shape to barn doors. NOTE: This is also common in northeastern Austria.

Ostrava.text: While possible to find in most of the country, blue street signs are more common in the east of the country, with Ostrava being the only major city to mainly use them.

Brno.text: White street signs with red text are most commonly found in the eastern parts of the country. They can also be found in the southernmost parts. NOTE: Brno notably uses this design.

spotlight.text: Streets in downtown Prague are commonly paved with grey and white marble stones, which is also typical for Portugal. They’re often arranged in intricate square mosaics, but some sections are far more plain. NOTE: Similar pavement can be found in much lower volume in other towns too. Consider the apparent size of the city before guessing Prague.
Pairs of black and white house numbers are found in Brno. NOTE: The city district can be found written on the black house number.

Red house numbers with a dividing line and a Roman numeral are unique to Liberec. The dividing line is an important identifying factor, as Roman numerals can be found on house numbers in other cities.

DK.name: Denmark
DK.key_meta: Denmark's bollards are white with a yellow reflector and a distinctive dark orange stripe at the top.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Denmark's bollards are white with a yellow reflector and a distinctive dark orange stripe at the top.
metas.comparison: Belgium's bollards are similar but have a rectangular reflector and no orange stripe at the top.

metas.title: Piped signs
metas.description: This signpost, where the pipe frame is bent around the sign, is unique to Denmark.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Street name ending - vej
metas.description: Most Danish street names end in "vej," which means "street" in Danish. Street signs typically have a blue background with white text.

metas.title: Town Signs
metas.description:
This unique sign is found when entering a town.
When leaving, there will be a red slash through the sign.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Square Roadlines
metas.description:
Outer road lines often consist of small white squares.
These unique-looking lines are a good way to identify Denmark.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Vej
metas.description:
Most Danish street names end in “vej.”
This is the Danish word for “street.”
Street signs most commonly have a blue background with white text.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe. This bollard is unique to the country. You may also find this green variant.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Belgium has bollards that may look somewhat similar. However, it will never feature the orange stripe.

metas.title: Landscape
metas.description:
Denmark is a generally flat country with wide, open fields between towns.
Suburban areas are usually open, with space between buildings.
Urban cores are more dense and built up.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Thatched & Corrugated Roofs
metas.description:
Some houses in Denmark have thatched roofs, especially in rural areas.
You can also sometimes find grey corrugated roofs.
These look somewhat similar to roofs commonly found in Baltic countries.

metas.title: 3Denmark
metas.description: Denmark's guy has a chill walking posture and has rounded edges on the person. Often found on thicker, 3D blue squares. His arms are also pointed down, unlike some similar signs found in Scandinavia.

metas.title: Direction Signs
metas.description:
Denmark has very unique-looking direction signs that are very useful to recognize the country.
They are low to the ground and framed by pipes.
They are either coloured red and white or blue and white, with a directional arrow incorporated into the background.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

general_rules.text: Denmark has an easy to learn road numbering system. They order their roads from east to west. Roads starting with the numbers 2 to 5 are grouped by region. Roads starting with the number 1 can be found nationwide, but the second digit still follows a rough regional distribution. Notably, Bornholm only has roads starting with the number 1. You can click on the image to enlarge it.

Copenhagen.text: Ring roads are special highways near bigger cities, labelled from O1 up to O4. The number increases from the centre, and each fully or partially encircles the city. These cities have ring roads: Copenhagen, Odense, Aarhus, Aalborg, Hillerød, Kolding, and Velje.

spotlight.text: The bus stops on the island of Bornholm have this unique green, red and white colour scheme.
These green bicycle signs are found on the island of Bornholm.

DO.name: Dominican Republic
DO.key_meta:
A Street View car with a white front and a roof rack filled with thick black rubber stripes is unique to the Dominican Republic.
Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.

metas.title: Unique car
metas.description:
A Street View car with a white front and a roof rack filled with thick black rubber stripes is unique to the Dominican Republic.
Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.
metas.comparison: With this landscape - similar cars can be found in Guatemala and Curaçao, but they lack the thick black stripes.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
A Learnable Meta World - Google Cars - Beginner
A Learnable Meta World - Google Cars - Basics

Coveragemap.text: Street View coverage in the Dominican Republic is very limited. Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.

Landscape.text: If you have mountains to the North, you will always be in Santiago de los Caballeros. NOTE: Although some parts of Santo Domingo are hilly, you will never see proper mountains like this one.
This type of landscape is found on the outskirts of Santo Domingo. It is characterised by narrow dirt tracks, whitish dirt, dried green shrubbery and debris next to the road.

Santiago.text: Yellow traffic light poles are typically found in the city of Santiago de los Caballeros. NOTE: This only applies to traffic light poles - yellow signposts are common in both cities.

Santo.text: As the capital and largest city, Santo Domingo has a more developed downtown area, with tall buildings and wide avenues.
Street name signs in Santo Domingo often contain the letters “ADN”, a reference to the Distrito Nacional, which the city is located in.
These black-and-purple pole markings are only found on poles in the Santo Domingo area.

spotlight.text: A small portion of the coverage in Santo Domingo was taken late in the evening. Similar imagery does not exist in Santiago de los Caballeros. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

EC.name: Ecuador
EC.key_meta: Ecuador is one of the countries in South America that uses bollards extensively, making them quite common in the country.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Ecuador is one of the countries in South America that uses bollards extensively, making them quite common in the country. There are two main types of bollards:
metas.comparison: While other types of bollards can be found, they almost always follow the same color scheme and style.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner

metas.title: Ecuador shitcam
metas.description: If you have vibes that you are in South America and coverage was taken using "shitcam" camera you gonna be in Ecuador. There is "shitcam" in other countries but in South America you can only find "shitcam" in Ecuador.
metas.comparison: Note: Ecuador also has GEN3(and little bit of GEN4) coverage not only shitcam! So don't discard Ecuador if it's not shitcam.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Intermediate

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description: Ecuador is one of the few Latin American countries where bollards are very common.
metas.comparison: You will find two main types of bollards: A round bollard with two red stripes, A flat bollard with two red reflectors on black. Many other bollards can be found, however, they will almost always have the same colour scheme and style. NOTE: A similar rectangular bollard can sometimes be found in Malaysia.

Coverage.text: Most of the coverage in Ecuador is centred around the western part of the country. A large part of the Amazon rainforest has no coverage. There is also some trekker coverage on the Galapagos Islands. You can check out the extent of the official coverage on this website.

Ecuagen43.text: Generation 4 coverage is found in most of Ecuador, with notable gaps in the northwest and southeast.

Relief.text: This is an elevation map of Ecuador. The imposing Andes mountains run through the middle of the country. The east and west of the country are more flat.

Banana.text: Banana plants, and especially plantations, are most commonly found in the southwestern part of the country.

Dry.text: This extremely dry landscape is only found in the coastal region between Guayaquil and Manta.

Flat.text: The flattest region is located around the city of Guayaquil. This is most easily seen on the E-25 and E-48. The Amazon area is also very flat, and will be described below.

Amazon.text: The Amazon area is very distinct. It is fairly flat, and contains many of these trees with white bark (Cordia trichotoma), and oil palms. The vast majority of the coverage notably uses the rarer “high antenna”.

Esmeraldes.text: The province of Esmeraldas can look similar to the Amazon region, but it is significantly hillier.

Southernregion.text: The southern regions have many winding mountain roads and exposed brownish red dirt. The central provinces can have similar roads, but the exposed dirt will usually not be found in these areas.

Chimborazo.text: The province of Chimborazo is semi-arid, and has an abundance of pine trees.

spotlight.text: The E-40 between Salinas and Guayaquil is one of the only divided highways in Ecuador, and the only one in the dry area near the southwestern coast.
A brown pipe can be seen on the side of a few north-eastern Ecuadorian roads.

The Galapagos Islands are an archipelago located west of mainland Ecuador. There are only trekkers and boat coverage on and around the islands. There is a wide variety of landscapes, including volcanic soil, low shrubbery, and craters (with Galapagos turtles onlooking). To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

EG.name: Egypt
EG.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (8 regions covered).

Pyramids.text: The great pyramids of Giza have trekker coverage. NOTE: This is not to be confused with the pyramid in Memphis, which is made of glass instead of sand stone.

Khafretemple.text: The coverage inside the valley temple of Khafre can be recognised by the rows of massive square pillars.

Djoser.text: The Djoser pyramid, which can be recognised by the stair-like sections combined with the scaffolding surrounding it, is located south of Cairo. You can also find some other minor historical excavation sites and some plain desert coverage.

Citadel.text: The Cairo Citadel is an enormous fortification with a trekker walking through and around it. It can be recognized by its massive walls that are made of clean-cut sandstone blocks.

Inside the Citadel, you can see the Ottoman-era Mosque of Muhammad Ali. It has light grey domes and very tall minarets. NOTE: This mosque looks superficially similar to the Hagia Sophia mosque in Istanbul.

Hanging.text: The trekker in and around the Hanging Church consists of two parts that look fairly different from each other. Outside the church, the trekker is walking around a normal urban Cairo street. At most points, you will still see the church complex, its spires with crosses, and historic sandstone walls. But you will also see apartment buildings, shops, and normal pedestrian traffic. This trekker can be found just east of Giza, near the map label Fustat.
At a certain point, the trekker moves from the street into the Hanging Church. Inside, you will see a beautiful courtyard with religious mosaics and two white church spires.

Quaitbay.text: The Qaitbay Citadel consists of a large castle surrounded by thick walls, which are both made of sandstone.

Saintmina.text: The monastery complex of Saint Mina consists of several large, palace-like buildings in a somewhat modern, Arabic style. Most of the buildings have several spires crowned with Christian crosses.

Abumena.text: The Abu Mena Heritage Site is a major excavation area southwest of Alexandria, just south of the Saint Mina monastery. In the middle of the site, you can find a small, yellow wooden chapel.

EE.name: Estonia
EE.key_meta: In Estonia, the words for street and road are "tänav" and "tee," respectively.

metas.title: Street name ending - tee
metas.description: In Estonia, the words for street and road are "tänav" and "tee," respectively. If you see street signs ending in "tee" or "tn" (with "tänav" often abbreviated as 'tn'), you know you're in Estonia.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Round bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back, which can be either white or orange, are common. Latvia's bollards might look similar, but they have a "half-circle" or flat curved shape, and sometimes feature numbers on them.

metas.title: Kilometre Markers
metas.description: All Baltic countries use the same blue kilometre marker.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Estonia Detailed 3 Stripes
metas.description: 3 Zebra Stripes: Estonia, Lithuania, Russia, Ukraine. Neck / Shoes / Detailed outline is unique to Estonia.

metas.title: Square Poles
metas.description:
You can additionally find a fair amount of square concrete poles, often also with diagonal supports.
These are similar to those found in Lithuania.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description:
Estonian bollards have a round, baton-like shape.
They have a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back.
The reflectors can be white or orange.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: No Border Signs
metas.description:
Each Baltic country has a slightly different border for its warning and speed signs.
Estonian signs have a thin red border, with no white outline around it.
The red border extends all the way to the edge of the sign.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Wood & White Brick
metas.description:
Estonian architecture generally consists of a combination of wood and white brick, typically with somewhat steep corrugated metal roofs.
Painted stone walls are also somewhat common.
While wooden buildings can be found in all three Baltic countries, they are more common in Estonia.

And.text: Estonia is a fairly flat country throughout, with only 10% of the country being higher than 100 metres, and the highest point being 318 metres tall. Still, the hilly parts can sometimes be recognizable. The hilliest areas are in the southeast, and the southern half of Lääne-Viru County. Note that the colours of this map are highly exaggerated to show the location of the hills more clearly.

Russian.text: Estonia has a large Russian minority. In most of Ida-Viru County, they form a majority. As a result, you will sometimes see bilingual signs with Russian Cyrillic and Estonian in the region in and around Narva. Note that the majority of signs will still be in Estonian. You may occasionally see Cyrillic in other places.

spotlight.text: The old town of Tallinn looks very different from any other urban area in Estonia. It is an almost perfectly preserved historic area, with lots of medieval and renaissance-era buildings. In places, it can look a lot like cities in central Europe.

Kihnu is a small island off the coast that has recognizable coverage: All coverage is Generation 4, taken during late autumn (recognizable by the fallen brown leaves on the ground). All coverage is Generation 4, taken during late autumn (recognizable by the fallen brown leaves on the ground). Noticeably, it has a very moody, dark cloud cover, taken close to sunset. Noticeably, it has a very moody, dark cloud cover, taken close to sunset. If you see a combination of these two things, Kihnu is a good place to guess. NOTE: Near Tartu you can also get a fair amount of autumn coverage, sometimes with a fair amount of cloud cover.

SZ.name: Eswatini
SZ.key_meta: Eswatini’s landscape is characterized by green, wooded hills and tall golden grass.

metas.title: Vibes
metas.description: Eswatini’s landscape is characterized by green, wooded hills and tall golden grass. Poles are made of dark brown wood and have a simple design, with insulators mostly mounted on the side.
metas.comparison: You can confirm it's Eswatini by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north. The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

Landscape.text: Montane grasslands with long golden grass and a mountainous landscape are typical of Western Eswatini. NOTE: Long grass can be found in almost all areas of Eswatini. This clue refers specifically to the pristine golden colour most commonly seen in the Western highlands.

This distinct region in the central South of the country, mostly along the MR9, can be recognized by the dark, overwhelming greenness and tall wooded mountains. NOTE: If you are struggling to see why this is unique, try comparing this to other areas of the country, which are more “golden” and light-coloured.
You can recognise this region in the east of the country thanks to the unusual flatness and the mountains often visible in the distance.

Pine.text: Pine tree plantations are found in select areas in the West of the country. NOTE: Similar plantations can also be found in South Africa.

Sugar.text: Sugar cane is grown in several areas along the Eastern border.

spotlight.text: The MR3 South of Ngomane can be recognized thanks to flatness, long dry grass and the dirt on the camera.
The MR3 from Manzini to the South African border is divided by metal and stone guardrails, making it recognisable. NOTE: This road is the only divided highway found in Eswatini.
The MR8 in Southeastern Eswatini straddling the South African border is recognisable because of this distinct ridge to the east.
You can recognise the Mlawula Nature Reserve thanks to the narrow dirt tracks, tall grass and overall savannah landscape.

If you see Portuguese text in Eswatini, you are most likely in the small town of Lomahasha. NOTE: This is because of its proximity to Mozambique, where Portuguese is spoken. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

FK.name: Falkland Islands
FK.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (1 regions covered).

Falklands.text: The Carcass Island trekker can be recognized by the open plains, with the ocean clearly visible. The ground may also get rocky. NOTE: Do not get this confused with the Faroe Islands trekker.
Open plains with slightly yellow grass can be seen on West Point Island. The ocean will not be clearly visible on this trekker.
This boat trekker can be seen in the West Point Bay, with yellow hills in the distance with the MS National Geographic Explorer in the bay with the trekker.
This sandy beach with other people in red and blue jackets can be seen on New Island.
Inland New Island can be recognized by the dark brown soil. Tire tracks may also be visible.
Distinct steep cliffs can be seen on New Island. To report inaccuracies, suggest new clues or give general feedback about our content, please use this form: https://www.plonkit.net/feedback

FO.name: Faroe Islands
FO.key_meta: No country-wide identifier found — see Regional (1 regions covered).

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description: Faroese bollards are small wooden sticks that are mainly painted yellow and sometimes red on the top.

metas.title: Above Ground Basements
metas.description:
Faroese houses are typically made of wood, often with an above ground basement made of stone which is painted in a different colour than the wooden part.
Roofs will usually be either metal or have grass on top (turf).

metas.title: Landscape
metas.description:
The landscape of the Faroe islands is characterised by long, wide fjords with jagged green mountains that rise straight out of the water, with rocky ridge lines along the mountainsides.
The mountains generally look more imposing and greener than coastal mountains in Iceland, which can often be used to tell them apart.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

Torshavn.text: Torshavn is by far the biggest town on the islands, and the only place where you will find buildings taller than three floors. The landscape is somewhat open relative to the rest of the country, particularly to the east.

spotlight.text: Klaksvik is the second biggest town in the country by a significant margin and can often be recognized by the narrow fjord with fairly steep hills going roughly north to south.
There are three wind parks visible on the Faroes. The largest one by far is northwest of Torshavn, while the other two are northeast of Torshavn and east of Vestmanna respectively.
The village of Kirkjubøur at the southern tip of the main island can be recognised by the black houses, almost all having grass roofs. The town also has a small church ruin.

FI.name: Finland
FI.key_meta: Street signs in Finland typically have a white background with black text, and most street names end in "tie.".

metas.title: Street name ending - tie
metas.description: Street signs in Finland typically have a white background with black text, and most street names end in "tie."

metas.title: Direction Signs
metas.description: Finnish directional signs consist of a solid blue background, white text, and a white border with guiding arrows.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Bollards
metas.description: Bollards in Finland are always completely black and white. They have a white rectangular reflector on the front and two white dots on the back. The black stripe is slightly angled.
metas.comparison: They come in two shapes: Hollow, thin and curved Round, baton-like shape Baltic/Nordic bollard infographic

metas.title: Snow Pole
metas.description: Orange snow pole with a thin white band near the top is commonly found in Finland. Norway/Sweden uses similar version but they have much wider white band (or even sometimes multiple ones).

metas.title: Architecture
metas.description:
Finnish architecture is mostly modern and utilitarian.
Downtown areas tend to be very modern, with lots of apartment buildings and use of concrete.
Suburbs mostly consist of freestanding single family homes.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Five Stripe Finland
metas.description: Detailed man without a hat and 5 Zebra stripes is Finland. Features both the detailed man's outline and the bold rounded, non-detailed person. Finland's bold non-detailed man with 5 zebra stripes has one arm pointed up, unlike Denmark.

general_rules.text: Finnish regional roads have 3- or 4-digit road numbers. The first digit of those road numbers is region-specific. These regions are distributed in a rough south-to-north order, starting from 1 in the south to 9 in the north. These road numbers often appear on direction signs. Learning the regions can help with cutting down on scanning time for 5k’s, or give you a rough region to plonk in during quick no move games. NOTE: Major roads with 2-digit road numbers do not adhere to this geographic pattern.

Lapland.text: Snow poles which have 2 long reflectors can be found on bigger roads in Lapland. NOTE: They can only be found in coverage from 2023 onward.

Generation 3 snow coverage is only found in far northwestern Lapland. NOTE: Be careful: this tip is specifically about regular Generation 3 coverage. Generation 2, 4, and trekker snow coverage can be found elsewhere.

spotlight.text: Downtown Helsinki has a lot of Generation 4 sidewalk trekker coverage. NOTE: This tip is specifically about Generation 4 trekker coverage. Generation 3 sidewalk trekkers can be found in many other Finnish cities.
Helsinki features these unique green-and-yellow trams. NOTE: Tampere is the only other Finnish city with trams, but they are red instead of green and yellow.
The buses in and around Helsinki are typically blue-and-white, with a vertical split. Buses elsewhere can have the same colour scheme, so look for one of these logos on the bus.
The buses in and around Tampere are blue on the bottom and white on the top. The word ‘NYSSE’ is written on the sides of the buses.
Buses in Turku are uniquely yellow, with a white rear.
Buses in Oulu have a pink front.
You can find Red rectangular metallic plates with 7 golden or dark red coloured protrusions that form a rounded hexagon shape on houses, lamp posts, and signposts in Tampere.

FR.name: France
FR.key_meta: The French word for street is “rue”.

metas.title: Word for street - RUE
metas.description: The French word for street is “rue”. Street signs with "rue" can also be found in Belgium.

metas.title: Ladder Poles
metas.description:
In France, these concrete ladder poles are pretty common.
They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Spain can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description:
The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top.
A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.

metas.title: Blue sticker
metas.description: Small blue rectangular markings on utility poles are unique to France. They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.
from_maps: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner

metas.title: Weird roadlines
metas.description: These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two offset blocks, are unique to France. They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Road Numbers
metas.description: Small yellow signs displaying the road number, which typically starts with a “D”, are unique to France. They are commonly placed on top of directional signs or town entry signs.

metas.title: Architecture - Stone House / Red Rooftiles
metas.description: Can be found all over France, but mainly central and southern.
metas.comparison: Note by MB: What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)

metas.title: Long Dashed Outlines
metas.description: Typical French roads have long spaced out dashes on the outside.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Infrastructure - Lille Streetsign
metas.description: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

metas.title: Vegetation - Meditteranean Vegetation
metas.description: The vegetation near the South-East coast looks very Mediterranean.
metas.comparison: Note by MB: This is more of a vibe thing tbh.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Wind Turbine
metas.description: Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.

metas.title: Short Signposts
metas.description: Traffic signs with particularly short signposts are very common in France.
from_maps: A Learnable Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.title: Trekker - Boat Trekker
metas.description: Several cities along the Cote d'Azur host boat trekkers in their harbours.

metas.title: Landscape - La Beauce
metas.description: La Beauce is one of the flattest regions of France, located South of Paris.
metas.comparison:
Apart from the flatness of the area, the important thing to notice about the fields in the Beauce region is that they are industrialized. You will not see hedges around the fields like you could see in the West of France.
So, if you see very flat and industrialized fields with potatoes or cereals, you can be in this area. Still, the Paris hedge remains good because there are many fields North and East of Paris (but you will never get a 5K by guessing Paris out of fields).

metas.title: Landscape - Mountains
metas.description: The tallest mountains are found in the southeast and on the Spanish border.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Powder Blue Infrastructure
metas.description: Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

metas.title: Agriculture - Sunflower
metas.description: Sunflowers are mostly found in the southwest of the country, particularly around Toulouse.

metas.title: Agriculture - Lavender Fields
metas.description: Lavender fields can be found in the southeast, appearing as small grey bushes when not fully grown.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Montpellier Streetsign
metas.description: Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.

metas.title: Architecture - West Coast Architecture
metas.description: The houses along the West Coast, from Nantes to Bayonne are usually low, with white walls, and red roofs.

metas.title: Language - Occitan - Carriera
metas.description: Different dialects of Occitan use different words for 'road'. Carriera can be found in South Central France.

metas.title: Architecture - Black Shingle Roofs with Mountains
metas.description: Black shingle roofs are often found in the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

metas.title: Architecture - Brick House / Red Rooftiles
metas.description: Brick roofs with red rooftiles can be found in the North mostly. Sometimes, they're also found around Toulouse.
metas.comparison: Note by MB: With red tiles, Toulouse is an option, with black shingles, it isn't. What I find more useful to differentiate the roof types is the materials. "Black Roofs" are shingles, while "Red Roofs" are actual tiles (which can also get very dark)

metas.title: Language - Occitan - Carriero
metas.description: Different dialects of Occitan use different words for 'road'. Carriero can be found in South-Eastern Coastal France.

metas.title: South - Rounded Tiles
metas.description: Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.

metas.title: Language - Town Suffix: -brie
metas.description: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. -brie can be found in Seine-Et-Marne

metas.title: Architecture - Alpine Architecture
metas.description: Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive wooden elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Similar houses can be found in the touristic parts of Pyrenees.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Bordeaux Streetsign
metas.description: Small tables with 'Arrᵗ' written on a small separate sign, are found in Bordeaux, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.

metas.title: Language - Catalan
metas.description: The far southern department Pyrénées-Orientales, also known as Catalunya Nord (Northern Catalonia), uses Catalan on their various signage.
metas.comparison: It is closely related to both Spanish and French, with Ç being considerably more common than in French. The word for street is carrer.

metas.title: Vegetation - Stone Pine
metas.description: Stone pines are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads. You may however find them as north as Nantes.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Bordeaux Signpost
metas.description: In the outskirts of Bordeaux, you may find square traffic signposts with the Bordeaux shade of red, named after the wine grown in the region.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Red posts by themselves are not unique to Bordeaux, so apply this meta with caution.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Lyon Streetsign
metas.description: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the name of the suburb instead.

metas.title: Agriculture - Corn
metas.description: Corn fields are mostly located in the Western part of the country, as well as in some areas in the East of Paris, and around Lyon and Strasbourg.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Eure-et-Loir Sticker
metas.description: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a green sticker, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Paris Streetsign
metas.description: Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.
metas.comparison: NOTE: The simple rectangular form of the sign can be found in the towns nearby and rarely in other cities.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Yellow Front License Plates
metas.description: France can sometimes have yellow back license plates, especially in old coverage. Should you see several yellow plates on the front, you're probably near Luxembourg.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Thin B-Type Guardrail
metas.description: Thin B type guardrail, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on highways in the northern half of the country, often coming from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz.
metas.comparison: NOTE: On the highlighted sections, thin B can be the minority guardrail, and short sections of any highway will have no guardrails at all. It is also more common on smaller roads in the North, but less consistent as a clue.

metas.title: Belgian Border - Dark Red Bricks
metas.description:
Rows of dark red brick houses, most similar to Flemish architecture in Belgium, are unsurprisingly found near the Belgian border.
The individual bricks may be outlined by white mortar.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Marseille Streetsign
metas.description: Marseille’s street signs will usually feature the city’s emblem, a variation of the Greek cross. The white border will usually be interrupted at the top, even when the cross is absent.

metas.title: Fat White Border France
metas.description: Has 2 designs, one of them has no bent elbow on the left arm which is unique to France. The other is the standard Italy-styled one, but French pedestrian signs all share a fat white border not found elsewhere.

metas.title: Car Meta - Rare Antenna - Blue
metas.description: On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.
metas.comparison: The blue flag can be found in Bas-Rhin, Aube and the Correze/Haute-Vienne/Dordogne Tristate

metas.title: Infrastructure - Brown Signback
metas.description: Road signs where both the post and back are painted brown are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is square, however round signposts are equally common.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.title: Vegetation - Maritime Pine Forest
metas.description: Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines (pinus pinaster) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.

metas.title: Agriculture - Salt Farms
metas.description: Salt farms, which appear as flooded trenches with grass medians, are unique to the west coastal islands of Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron as well as the nearby coast, as well as some very niche areas in the South of France (Camargue).

metas.title: Paris - Uneven & Cream Colored Stones
metas.description:
Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris.
Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.

metas.title: Architecture - Mansard Roof
metas.description: Mansard roofs, also known as French windows, are a very common feature of Parisian architecture. They’re made up of steep black shingle roofs with inserted dormer windows. While not unique to Paris, it is a good clue in abundance and on wide boulevards.
metas.comparison: On some occasions, they can also be found in the North of France.

metas.title: Architecture - Basque Architecture
metas.description: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.
metas.comparison: NOTE: They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Cityname Roadsign
metas.description: Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the name of the city, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a modern design, and many city names will be river based, notably named after Seine and Marne.
metas.comparison: NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

metas.title: Toulouse - Architecture
metas.description:
In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings.
They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

metas.title: Landscape - Cote d'Azur
metas.description: The French Riviera (Cote d'Azur) will mirror many characteristics of Monaco. Rich areas with planted palms and light coloured multi story buildings with wide balconies are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.

metas.title: Language - Breton
metas.description: Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Pas-de-Calais Sign
metas.description: In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a dark green post paired with a signback of a lighter shade of green, ranging from matcha green to greenish turquoise. The department’s logo, a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present on the signback.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs. Also, beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

metas.title: Language - Basque
metas.description: Bilingual signs in Basque, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
metas.comparison: The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

metas.title: Language - Water Town Name
metas.description: Many French cities contain the name of the river they lay on, usually in the format -sur-[river]. On signage, sur are often shortened to ˢ/, in this case Chalonnes-sur-Loire (Chalonnes upon Loire). The picture shows five of the longest and therefore most common origins of river based names, but cities can bear the name of any river, regardless of length.
metas.comparison: Similarly, city names containing -sur-mer (=on sea) or -plage (=beach) are found exclusively on the coast.

metas.title: Language - Occitan
metas.description: Occitan is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on town entry signs. It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal dialect

general_rules.text: French telephone numbers are 10 digits long, with the first two pairs of digits being two separate area codes, following two patterns: 01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes clockwise from the northwest. 01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes clockwise from the northwest. 2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing anticlockwise. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast. 2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing anticlockwise. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast. Secondary area codes in Île-de-France can be seen on this map. NOTE: Phone numbers beginning with 06-09 are not regional.

Each department has an assigned number to it, arranged mostly alphabetically. This is most useful in postal codes, consisting of 5 digits, the first two representing the department they’re in. NOTE: the same regional codes are used inside the right blue strip on licence plates.

Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the name of the city, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a modern design, and many city names will be river based, notably named after Seine and Marne. NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.

Alsace.text: Streets containing German names are concentrated in Alsace.

Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region.

Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into architecture in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.
Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.

Brittany.text: Towns with the Plou- prefix are concentrated in Northwestern Brittany.

Dark green road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

On the Breton island Belle-Île-en-Mer you can find houses typical for Brittany combined with colourful façades and outlines, superficially similar to houses in Portugal.

NOTE: The entire island was only covered with an often oversaturated Generation 2 camera.

A greyish green signback supported by a darker green post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

NOTE: Beware that this, and other colored infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.

On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as Blue Coast), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.

NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly Brittany, so consider the landscape as well.

Brittany has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country.
Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stones surrounding doors and windows.
The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.

Dark green road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country. NOTE: Beware that this, and the following coloured infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.
A greyish green signback supported by a darker green post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.

Normandy.text:
Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.

NOTE: Hedges by themselves are not sufficient for recognizing this area and are common all over France.

Roads with a significant red, purple or burgundy tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.

NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.

It is not so rare to see cows, horses, or sheep in France in Geoguessr. If that ever happens, you should consider the West of the country (Brittany, Normandy), as well as the mountainous regions (Pyrenees and Alps). This is where you have the most chances to find animals in France in Google Street View.

Roads with a significant red, purple or burgundy tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of Burgundy, which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area. NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.

Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy. NOTE: Hedges by themselves are not sufficient for recognizing this area and are common all over France.

Corsica.text:
Cuboid barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.

NOTE: Stone barriers with a rounded top are not found on Corsica.

On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.

Cuboid barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape. NOTE: Stone barriers with a rounded top are not found on Corsica.

Centre.text:
Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river.
Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.

Champagne.text: France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area around Bordeaux, southern coast and Champagne, East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica.

France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area around Bordeaux, southern coast and Champagne, East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica. NOTE: This map is highly simplified, see this map for more detailed and extensive description.

Occitanie.text: A red and yellow logo with an Occitan cross and vertical stripes is the official flag of the Occitanie region. The rest of the regions also have logos, which appear less frequently. You can see them projected onto a map here.

Provence.text: A flag made up of red and yellow stripes, based on the Senyera, is the official flag and department logo of Pyrénées-Orientales. You will often find the pattern used in coats of arms on street signs. NOTE: The flag of Provence looks similar, but with vertical stripes instead.

spotlight.text: On the Breton island Belle-Île-en-Mer you can find houses typical for Brittany combined with colourful façades and outlines, superficially similar to houses in Portugal. NOTE: The entire island was only covered with an often oversaturated Generation 2 camera.

On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as Blue Coast), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, Cagnes-sur-mer, west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure. NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly Brittany, so consider the landscape as well.

DE.name: Germany
DE.key_meta: Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors.

metas.title: Bollard
metas.description: Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections. They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.
metas.comparison: NOTE: Many European countries have similar bollards, however most will have different coloured reflectors. Luxembourg uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.

metas.title: Language - Town Suffix: -itzsch
metas.description: The suffix -itzsch can be found in Eastern Germany.

metas.title: Language - Town Suffix: -schütz
metas.description: The suffix -schütz can be found in Eastern Germany.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Streetsigns - Essen
metas.description: Essen has blue signs with a very thick metallic frame.

metas.title: Infrastructure - Streetsigns - Mainz
metas.description: Mainz has a mix of blue signs, and this unique red variant.

metas.title: Landscape - Flat Landscape
metas.description: The North and especially Northwest of Germany is very flat.

metas.title: Language - Town Suffix: -a
metas.description: The suffix -a can be found in the Southern Half of Germany.

metas.title: Language - Town Suffix: -ach
metas.description: The suffix -ach can be found in the Southern Half of Germany.

metas.title: Gen 4
